subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEETING IN PARIS OF FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 9, I attended in Paris a meeting of finance ministers of the Group of Ten countries and of all members of the European Economic Community. The question before us was how best to relieve the speculative pressures affecting currency values which had led to the withdrawal of European and Japanese authorities from their exchange markets on March 2.
The meeting on Friday last permitted a useful exchange of views but could not arrive at any definite conclusions until the European countries had decided themselves whether to define fixed rates of exchange or to float and, if the latter, whether to float in unison or separately.
The Europeans made their own decisions Sunday night and, as is now known, beginning next Monday six countries will float jointly against the U.S. dollar; three others, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Italy, will for the time being float separately. Until next Monday, the European and Japanese markets will remain closed as they have been since March 2.
At a further meeting on Friday next which I shall be attending, there will be discussion of certain possibilities of co-operation between the European countries and others and we will no doubt discuss plans for expediting work now in train on the over-all reform of the monetary system.
Although the decisions taken last weekend do not have any direct, immediate consequences for Canada, I believe they will be helpful in reducing the speculative pressures that have been affecting certain exchange rates. By permitting the exchange rate system to react more directly to fundamental market forces, the decisions will set the stage for the basic reforms that are required.
Given Canada's great stake in foreign trade, we feel it is urgent to re-establish a calm, orderly international monetary regime and we shall participate actively in the international discussions and decisions directed to this vital objective.
This is a difficult time with respect to international trade and payments and much work lies ahead. While contributing all we can to the international discussions, we must make every effort to maintain the strength of our
industries so that they will be able to meet competition and provide jobs for Canadians.
I am tabling with your permission, Mr. Speaker, copies of the communique issued in Paris, Friday, March 9, by our Group of Ten meeting and of the communique issued by the meeting of finance ministers of the European Economic Community in Brussels, Sunday, March 11.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEETING IN PARIS OF FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are glad to see the minister with us today, knowing that he is making an interim report to cabinet. I would have hoped he would prepare a rather more informative statement for the House because, with all due respect, in many ways this statement is about as empty of real information as a good deal of the budget speech the minister made to the House some nights ago. Be that as it may, this conference, this meeting will perhaps mean in days to come that after some 25 years the principles of the Bret-ton Woods Agreement will be not only obsolescent in its present form but probably obsolete in that we have so many currencies now floating subject no doubt, as in Canada's case, to massive central bank intervention. We know that some 15 months ago the Bank of Canada did intervene massively when there was the prior crisis with regard to the United States dollar. It would be interesting to know how much intervention there is at the present time.
In the minister's statement we find the following:
By permitting the exchange rate system to react more directly to fundamental market forces, the decisions will set the stage for the basic reforms that are required.
I simply enter the following caveat in that regard: Subject to the degree of central bank intervention which may totally distort the operations of the true market forces. In the press release tabled by the minister there is one sentence in paragraph four which leaves me wondering a little whether the ministers who met during this past weekend have not tried to find some convenient excuse by saying that the crisis was due to the speculative movement of funds. That in itself is an oversimplification. It may well reflect an inability to resolve the massive trade imbalances that have existed in respect of the grouping of problems within the Common Market.
The minister has indicated that the ministers unanimously expressed a determination to ensure jointly an orderly exchange rate system. Surely to goodness this does not even set the stage for the opening of multilateral trade talks this fall when a good many of the problems that underlie the speculative shifts where there is a surplus of a certain kind of currency floating about will be dealt with. Hopefully, this coming weekend we will get better reasoning than that expressed in paragraph four of the minister's press release.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEETING IN PARIS OF FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my appreciation to the Minister of Finance for giving us an advance copy of his statement. I hope he enjoyed his trip to Paris because it does not seem that there was any other reason for it except enjoyment. There does not seem to be much of a contribution that Canada has either made or could have made. I do not see that much has been accomplished by the meeting. Six countries have agreed to tie their currencies together and to allow them to float together. This still does not eliminate the speculation that will take place against those currencies in the future unless those six countries think that their currencies are strong enough that they can keep this kind of a tie while at the same time keeping the speculators off.
I do not think there has been much improvement or that we can have much optimism about the future of currency movements in the world. It seems to me that the real problem of speculation is not being faced by the Group of Ten and the Common Market group, and certainly it does not seem to have been faced by the Canadian government. One of the very real problems that exists is the action of the multinational corporations and their role in international speculation. To that extent we would like to get some information about what the Canadian banks are doing in this speculative fever that exists in the world. We can talk about the gnomes of Zurich, but there are some very respectable gnomes running around with all kinds of hot money disrupting international markets.
I think it is important that at some point the Minister of Finance give us some indication on the matter of policing and monitoring Canadian-based multinational corporations such as Inco and Brascan. For instance, did he raise this question at the meeting, or was the question raised at all by the other countries? Is there any movement in the direction of doing something to control the multinational corporations throughout the world that seem to act as independent agents contrary to the interests of the governments of the countries themselves? Unless the minister tells us that he is dealing with these matters, we can only hope, as I said earlier, that he had a very nice time and a nice trip to Paris.

subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MEETING IN PARIS OF FINANCE MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all the problems arising today in the western world's different monetary systems almost make us, of the Social Credit Party, smile, because for many years we have precisely been denouncing such a system.
All currency fluctuations and related problems prove the impossibility of maintaining sound monetary balance within the present financial system. Each country, and that is the cause of the problem, wants to have a favourable commercial balance, which is materially impossible and leads to speculation on various currencies.
Mr. Speaker, all this happens because it is overlooked that money has no value except what it represents in goods or services. Canada should give the whole world a concrete example by establishing a monetary system truly based on the balance which should exist between currency on the one hand and production on the other. We would thus return to sound commercial transactions, by way of
exchanging goods rather than by meaningless currency fluctuations.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON BENEFIT CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I undertook to make a statement to the House on the benefit control program being applied to prevent payments of unemployment insurance benefits to persons not entitled under the act to receive them, and on the methods used by the Unemployment Insurance Commission to establish such errors and identify individual claimants who have been receiving such benefits.
Let me start by saying categorically that I am firmly convinced that the vast majority of Canadians now drawing unemployment insurance benefits are fully entitled to receive them by right of legislation enacted by parliament and by its true intent. I am equally determined that this majority of rightful claimants not be badgered or humiliated as a result of the commission's efforts to weed out the minority who, knowingly or unknowingly, are abusing the program.
Before outlining the ground rules by which unemployed Canadians are entitled to draw benefits, under the program described by the Canadian Labour Congress in its recent brief to the cabinet as "one of the best in the world," and the procedures now applied to ensure that this program and its reputation are not damaged by abuse, I can first report to hon. members two or three immediate steps that have been taken to protect rightful claimants against harassment.
At my request the Unemployment Insurance Advisory Committee, a nine-member body composed of four representatives of organized labour, four representatives of business, and Chairman Anatole Lesyk, Q.C., of Montreal, met this morning to undertake its own thorough study of the current benefit control operation, and other matters related to proposed amendments to the current act.
I can further report that all benefit control officers have been instructed that the need for thoroughness in their work does not and must not justify an overzealous approach or underhanded methods.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON BENEFIT CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON BENEFIT CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
3. The benefit control officer must recognize the particular circumstances of a claimant, and be prepared to assist those in need of help by referring them to the claimant assistance program.
If any hon. member of the House, on either side, knows of any specific instance in which these guidelines have been abused by officials of the commission, I would be grateful to receive any information that would help rectify any injustice.
But in fairness to the Unemployment Insurance Commission officials who have been under long and heavy pressure, first in the effort to design and put into operation a sweeping transformation and improvement of the unemployment insurance system and, second, to iron out the kinks that were unavoidable when changes so radical were made at the pace at which the new program was implemented, I must emphasize that my own investigation in the week since I committed myself to make this report to the House has not turned up any volume of specific instances of overzealousness.
Another measure I would like to say will come into being is the distribution of a pamphlet to all people drawing unemployment insurance benefits clearly setting forth their rights and obligations under the act and under the appeal system.
The duty of the benefit control officers is to detect violation of the law, and the law is quite clear. Section 25 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, reads as follows:
A claimant is not entitled to be paid benefit for any working day in an initial benefit period for which he fails to prove that he was either
(a)	capable of and available for work and unable to obtain suitable employment on that day, or
(b)	incapable of work by reason of any prescribed illness, injury or quarantine on that day.
Further, under Regulation 145 passed in July, 1972, all unemployment insurance claimants are specifically notified in writing, when they receive their first benefit payment, that they may be required to prove that they are actively seeking work. Registration with their local Canada Manpower Centre, or with their union hiring hall if this is the custom in their occupation, is required of all claimants. But this is not in itself in all cases sufficient proof of active search for a job, particularly in localities where suitable jobs are available but are not being filled.
With your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, I will digress here to urge all Canadian employers, and particularly those who have complained that the present unemployment insurance system has hampered their efforts to fill jobs, to register their vacancies with the Canada Manpower Centre. I cannot overemphasize the importance of this step in helping ensure that unemployed persons and unfilled jobs are quickly brought together.
Guided by information on job vacancies listed at Canada Manpower Centres, by the "help wanted" columns of newspapers and other local labour market information, offices of the Unemployment Insurance Commission implement Regulation 145 by sending job search statement forms to claimants whose occupational
Unemployment Insurance Benefit Control
skills are known to be in demand in the locality in which they live. These forms ask the claimant to list the dates and details of efforts made to find work since filing claim for benefits, the persons contacted, the location at which the application was made, the type of work sought, and the results of the effort.
I repeat, these forms are to be sent only to claimants whose skills are known to be in demand in the area in which they live. This more sophisticated method of sorting out, by region and occupation, those claimants whose job skills are in local demand went into full operation at the beginning of this year. Its development began in mid-1972.
It relies on two basic tools. The first is an exhaustive classification of occupations of claimants. Second, special computer programs based on this classification make it possible to check the number of unfilled job openings in any area against the number of unemployment insurance claimants in that area who could fill those specific vacancies.
This does not mean that unemployment insurance claimants are disqualified by a computer. The computer programming is only a tool that guides benefit control officers to individuals who are drawing unemployment insurance benefits while living in an area where their occupational skills are in high demand.
These individuals are then interviewed, as a rule at home, by a benefit control officer, to determine whether they have been actively seeking work and are genuinely available for work. A report of the interview is written, to be signed by the claimant. Most commonly the report is written by the benefit control officer but the claimant is free to make changes or additions before signing it, and is free to refuse to sign. The report is made in two copies, with one kept by the claimant.
In some cases the accuracy of the answers given by the claimant is checked out discreetly by the benefit control officer.
The statement of the benefit control officer, and his report of the results of any subsequent investigation, are turned over to an insurance officer who decides, according to the act and the regulations, whether the claimant is entitled to continue drawing benefits. If the decision is that disentitlement is warranted, the claimant has the right, and is so informed, to appeal to a board of referees. These boards are independent bodies. Each includes a representative of the labour movement, a representative of the employers, and a chairman appointed by the government. The claimant has the right to present new evidence, not given to the benefit control officer in the original interview, to the board. Proof of search for work since the interview may lead to re-entitlement.
The investigations undertaken under this system have been described as "blitzes". In fact, in the large urban centres they are part of a continuing process. Only in the smaller communities do teams of benefit control interviewers move in for short periods, each officer interviewing an average of six claimants a day.
The rate of disqualifications resulting from the benefit control process has been startling. In the first nine weeks
2154

March 13, 1973
Unemployment Insurance Benefit Control of 1973, of 62,879 claimants whose investigation was completed, 40,846, or 65 per cent, were disqualified.
It must be borne in mind that the number of completed investigations is only slightly more than 10 per cent of the total number of Canadians drawing unemployment insurance. Those investigated were pre-selected by the computer and classification system I have described. In areas where there are no jobs available, there are no investigations.
I take no satisfaction from this high rate of disqualification.
Few hon. members would quarrel with the results of an investigation in which it was learned that 32 claimants, normally residents of Calgary and Edmonton, had asked the commission during the height of the skiing season to mail their unemployment insurance cheques to a post office box which proved to be the address of the Banff Springs Hotel. Twenty-nine of them were disqualified.
But in the more common cases this process of investigation and disqualification when it is warranted is an unpleasant necessity. The existing Unemployment Insurance Commission was established to help Canadians afflicted by unemployment, not to hound or harass them. The benefit of any doubt must still go to the individual.
The program cannot, however, fulfil its goal of helping the genuinely unemployed maintain a decent life unless it is both fair and seen to be fair. It must be fair to the unemployed who are sincere in wanting work, to the employees and employers who pay premiums, and to the Canadian taxpayers, who pay a substantial share of its cost in times of high unemployment.
It is to protect this essential condition of the program's survival, and guard its acceptability in the eyes of the majority of Canadians, who will support a generous program if they are assured that it is not being abused and exploited, that these new and more effective benefit control procedures have been developed and put into effect.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for giving me ample time to at least peruse the statement he has made in order for me to be able to make some comments. I certainly welcome the statement, subject to certain matters which I will bring to the minister's attention.
I am pleased to note the minister has indicated there will be no badgering or unnecessary harassment of those who are entitled to claims. I was pleased to hear the minister state that the program "must be fair to the unemployed who are sincere in wanting work, to the employees and employers who pay premiums, and to the Canadian taxpayers, who pay a substantial share of its cost in times of high unemployment." Another paragraph in the minister's statement is even more significant: "It is to protect this essential condition of the program's survival and guard its acceptability in the eyes of the majority of Canadians, who will support a generous program if they are assured that it is not being abused and exploited, that these new and more effective benefit control procedures have been developed and put into effect."
As I listened to the minister trying to justify the unjustifiable, it took me back to the days when this act was first

brought before the House of Commons. At that time, we on this side indicated to the minister that there was something wrong with the act in view of the fact it amalgamated or integrated insurance and welfare. We stated that as a result there would be significant problems, the likes of which we did not know. Now we do know what it is all about.
I was not only surprised but flabbergasted when I read of the investigation that took place in the Hamilton-Toron-to area where some 20,000 out of 28,000 investigated were either disqualified or threatened with disqualification. I am not a mathematician, but that seems to be approximately 70 per cent. That is a far cry from the 3 per cent or 4 per cent we have been told were cheating. I do not have any qualms about the type of language I use. Cheaters and chisellers must go. This is the cry of all members of the House and the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON BENEFIT CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Hear, hear!

My friends to the left may say that is a right wing philosophy, but we are talking about tax dollars and trying to make a very difficult act work. When we were on the hustings during the election campaign, we stated we would like to bring in the Auditor General in order to ascertain how much the Unemployment Insurance Act is costing the people. We have since heard it is some $2 billion. We also indicated that abuses should be cut down. In this regard I am pleased to see we are moving in that direction. We also stated we would tighten up the administration. All these things are now coming into focus.
I do not want it left that, through overzealousness on the part of benefit control officers, those who are rightfully entitled will be cut off to their detriment. It seems to me that the way in which we are now approaching this matter is a proper way as long as we understand it should be done with compassion and understanding for those rightfully in need.
There is also the problem of the appeal board. I respectfully suggest that the minister must direct his attention to this area because I heard him say there has not been a significant number of appeals since the investigations began. However, I can vouch for the fact there will be appeals for the simple reason the act allows for appeals. There will be those who, through some quirk of fate, overzealousness or for some other reason are denied benefits and when they are denied they will take advantage of the appeal procedures under the act.
I note that the minister, as promised, has referred this question to the advisory committee. I understand, also, that he has referred other matters to that committee in connection with proposed amendments to the existing act. I hope that in due course the minister will enlighten the House as to these other matters, related to the Unemployment Insurance Act, which he has directed to the committee's attention in order that we may know just what is being studied.
Of equal concern to me is the fact that the minister, in order to show some awareness of the problem, did introduce Bill C-125 but has not referred it to the standing
March 13, 1973

committee to provide Members of Parliament as well as representatives of labour, employers and other concerned people with an opportunity to become involved in discussion of this legislation. It now seems to me, from the announcements I have heard, that the minister is attempting to amend the act by way of administrative or ministerial directive rather than giving representatives of labour, management and other groups, as well as Members of Parliament, the opportunity to delve into the subject matter of this bill.
I notice, also, that a report is still awaited from the advisory committee. The minister did not tell us whether this report was needed before he would introduce a modified or amended Bill C-125. I wish he had cleared up this point, because I should like to see a bill of some kind introduced rather than action be taken by way of administrative direction. The former course would allow hon. members to give the minister the benefit of their expertise.
In giving direction to the benefit control officers the minister indicated that these officers must recognize the particular situation in which claimants find themselves and assist those in need of help. Many people in Canada fall into this latter category; because of difficulty in adjusting to language or culture they are left at some disadvantage. I hope the minister realizes that in certain areas, particularly in our larger urban areas, this can be a serious problem. A great many people really do not know what is going on, and because of harassment in the past they are often afraid of the type of person who is involved in carrying out these inquiries. I hope that in our major urban centres, to which most of our immigrants are attracted, this situation will be kept carefully in mind and that those concerned will be treated with understanding.
The minister talked about availability for work and suitability for employment. I hope he realizes that in many instances people go across this land looking for work in all sincerity, but because of gentlemen's agreements, shall we say, based on attitudes toward sex, race or colour, they are denied employment. I see the minister shaking his head. This is something else we have to be extremely careful about; I hope the benefit control officers are aware that such a situation does exist in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I see I am running out of time.

speechtext:
It waxes strange that this government, which created high unemployment in order to fight inflation, which was responsible for this monster that it let loose among the Canadian people, had to do something about the large numbers who became unemployed and brought the new Unemployment Insurance Act into being. We in this party applauded that act because it took care of and looked after the interests of those who had become the victims of the massive war against inflation that created unemployment.
We in this party have never condoned the actions of those who cheat in any social or corporate program. We fully realize, as studies will verify, that about 2 per cent of the people affected cheat in any social program. The minister himself, in his statement, said he is firmly convinced that the vast majority of Canadians now drawing unemployment insurance benefits are fully entitled to receive those payments as of right according to law. Having said that, he went on to pick out one small example among the minority of claimants and referred to people in Calgary or Edmonton who went skiing and had their unemployment insurance cheques mailed to them. If he is so concerned about the rights of those who have an entitlement to unemployment insurance being criticized in the press, why has he lampooned a small number of those who are collecting unemployment insurance incorrectly? We suggest that this statement will only serve to reinforce the reactionary thinking of those who are against the vast numbers of people legally collecting unemployment insurance.
This party has never faulted the act and what it seeks to do, nor the broadening of the act which is necessary to cover those who are the victims in this war. Yet we do criticize the administration of the act. We feel that the act is administered in a very inhumane fashion.
May I speak briefly about the benefit control officers. Apparently the minister has instructed them to follow three particular aspects of a certain code of ethics. The minister may not be aware of some of the questions that are being asked. As recently as last week I learned of a fellow who had been a university lecturer and had earned $10,000 a year for two years. He became unemployed following a cutback in university spending. He was laid off and collected unemployment insurance. Then he was visited by a benefit control officer who asked him what salary he would accept. The man answered, "$10,000 a year", because that was the salary he had earned for the past two years. One week later he received notification from the commission saying that he was limiting his opportunities for employment by saying he would accept only $10,000 a year and his unemployment insurance benefits were cut off. That is only one example. I could list many such examples. I deal with 52 unemployment

insurance cases a week involving my local office. I will gladly give the minister several examples showing that the administration of the act is at fault.
This party has always held that social programs such as unemployment insurance exist to help people. The Unemployment Insurance Act is supposed to help them over the rough stages until they can again obtain employment. Instead, we find, that they are being used to feed reactionary thinking across the country. What the government ought to do to solve this problem is expand the economy so that jobs will be created and there will be an opportunity for anyone wanting work to obtain a job.
The only thing we applaud in the statement of the minister is his intention to have the advisory committee of the UIC take a look at the whole matter of benefit control and the way in which it is implemented across the country. We support that aspect of the program. The rest of the statement, I repeat, concerns a small number of claimants and that part of it merely feeds the fires of reactionary thinking among members to my right.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON BENEFIT CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot help mentioning first that we have received the statement in English. I accept the apologies of the minister, but I would point out to him that one way of reducing unemployment would be to hire more translators.
I also wish to say that temporary amendments such as those suggested will not solve the problem. The legislation is too complicated and is difficult to put into effect. The Canadian people do not understand legislation which is too complicated. Mistakes have increased last winter and it was worse this winter. Some workers waited three months before being paid; I met some during the weekend who filed claims at the end of November and who have not yet been paid.
I do not necessarily criticize the public servants, because I admit that some are good; they are not all good but several are conscious of their responsibilities. However they are administering an almost unworkable piece of legislation due to all kinds of administrative complexities which the workers cannot easily understand.
I have already mentioned this in committee but not too often, because I do not monopolize the time allotted to others. However, I would like legislation prepared for workers to be drawn up in terms clear enough to enable them to understand it.
I will not dwell on this matter now; I suppose that an amendment to the legislation will be introduced. I feel that another bill should be brought in to clear up the situation.
One important point that must be borne in mind is decentralization. Centralization of benefit payments in one regional office has resulted in the installation of com-
March 13, 1973

puters which should hasten the solution to late payments. Thousands of unemployed go through an unfortunate experience in this field. They must wait for months, as I said earlier, before getting their first benefit cheque. This situation is inconceivable not to say revolting.
I suggest here that payments ought to be made in district offices and if the government really wants to improve the fate of thousands of unemployed, it must take some practical means, including decentralization. This is why I insist that they ought to introduce clearly written legislation and prepare regulations enabling understanding officials-and I know that some of them are-to truly assist the unemployed by administering in a humane way social legislation. Public servants would do well to remember that they are the servants of the people not despots, that a nation is made up of individuals not robots. The unemployed may be without work but not necessarily without sense. They see what is happening. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 56-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
That this House deplores the failure of the government to develop beyond the 1965 Canada-United States Automotive Agreement a policy which would benefit Canadians and which would contribute to resolving Canada-United States conflict in this area to the mutual benefit of both countries; and this House, therefore, urges the government to take certain immediate steps to lower the prices of automobiles to Canadian consumers and to protect the jobs of Canadian auto workers.
He said: Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago today the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) sparked a two day flurry of controversy on the meaning and importance of the Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement.
At the heart of the controversy three related items are to be found, each of which emerged during the two day debate or discussion but which were unresolved. First, there was the interest of Canadian consumers who have paid, cumulatively, hundreds of millions of dollars more than they should for North American automobiles since 1965. Second, there was the concern of thousands of Canadian auto workers who for approximately three years have been left by a vacillating government in a state of uncertainty about the future of their jobs. Third, there was and is the crucial matter of United States government dissatisfaction with the results of the automotive agreement. This dissatisfaction was formally conveyed just a few days ago in a television interview by Senator Hartke 
of Indiana. Surrounding these three areas of concern, indeed, making them inextricably bound one to the other, is the nature, meaning and relevance of what are known as the safeguards in the Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement.
There can be no doubt that the two Liberal governments elected in January, 1968 and again last October 30 must bear the major share of the blame for the apprehension which exists among many of our workers in this industry, for the gouging of Canadian consumers and, to a much lesser but real extent, for the dissatisfaction of the Americans.
For over three years now the government, for political reasons, has deliberately involved itself in a contradictory approach, as evidenced by statements, to the Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement. On the one hand, it has not yielded to United States pressure to remove the safeguards from the Agreement; yet, at the same time, it has tacitly accepted the American view by implying in its public statements that the safeguards built into the pact were either transitional from the outset or, in any case, were no longer required. Neither Canadians nor Americans know the real policy of this government on this industry.
The former minister of industry, trade and commerce took great care never to say in public that he regarded the safeguards as being transitional, although in private he frankly said that his commitment to this view was somewhat less than 100 per cent. However, the present minister blew the whistle, I think, on what I consider to have been the real government policy for the past two years when he said in the House two weeks ago that the safeguards were transitional. During the subsequent two days of exchanges in this House, the minister was forced to correct his earlier assertion and admit on March 1 that he had been in error when he said that it was stated in the auto pact that the safeguards were transitional. It is good that the minister corrected the public record. It is even more important, however, for the government to tell the people of Canada what its automotive policy is. What are its plans for Canadian consumers and Canadian auto workers? What is it presenting in the ongoing negotiations to the Americans for discussion? Is it presenting anything, or is it simply, as I suspect, reacting to American initiatives?
The auto pact came into being in 1965 following years of deficits amounting to hundreds of millions of dollars annually on Canada's part in Canada-United States automotive trade. Prior to its signing, the Canadian government had decided to embark on an export subsidy plan, to correct this major trade balance problem. Understandably, at that time the American government did not favour this kind of unilateral action aimed in its direction. That program, incidentally, was exactly equivalent to the United States DISC program, which the United States has imposed on the rest of the world in the past year.
At that time, instead of accepting Canadian proposals to go ahead with this unilateral trade action, the United States agreed to hold talks with Canada. Those talks centred on the need to improve Canada's balance of trade position. That improvement would provide for the
March 13, 1973

future growth of the North American automobile industry in this country and in the United States. The result of those discussions was the auto pact. The intent of the pact was to liberalize automotive trade between Canada and the United States by removing most tariff barriers and ensuring that the industry in both countries would be able "to participate on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total market of the two countries", as provided in Article 1(b) of the Canada-U.S. Automotive Agreement.
In exchange for two basic commitments, the government of Canada agreed to permit automotive companies located in our country to import cars and parts from the United States. The commitments or, as they are now known, the safeguards, were: First, United States auto makers were obliged to continue, as a minimum, to produce the number of vehicles in Canada bearing the same ratio to their sales in Canada as in the base year 1964; second, in addition each company was required to provide an increasing amount of what is now known as Canadian value added. This consists of the dollar value of labour and parts produced on the Canadian side of the border. The amount of increase was to grow proportionately for each year in the future.
Both countries hoped to gain from this arrangement. The Americans would gain tariff free access to a very lucrative Canadian market. This would enable the car companies to rationalize their production runs on a continental basis and thus put them in a more competitive position in both countries vis-a-vis cars produced outside our continental North America. Canada gained by having in the second safeguard an assurance that our trade balance in automotive products with the United States would no longer be in permanent deficit, and we would be sure of our share of any growth in jobs in the industry in this country. The third beneficiary would have been the Canadian consumer, who was to get a substantial reduction in automotive prices as a result of the removal of tariffs to the companies. These tariff concessions were to be given on the condition the companies met certain conditions to which I just referred. The companies, however, made the individual consumer pay an extra duty.
What have been the results of the pact since 1965, Mr. Speaker? Canada's position in the North American automotive trade has certainly improved. We have moved from a chronic deficit position to one of having a slight surplus last year of $5.8 million. Cumulatively-I stress this-for the period 1965-1972, we experienced, nevertheless, a net deficit in North American automotive trade of about $2 billion. One can hardly say that the pact has brought miraculous benefits to Canada. If the present trend in the trade graph continues, next year will almost certainly show another deficit.
Employment in the industry has also grown. In 1964, there were about 70,000 employees in Canada. In this industry about 97,000 are now employed. Similar growth in employment has taken place in the United States. The Canadian consumer, however, has not obtained his fair share of the intended benefits of the pact. After allowing for differences in tax structures between the two countries, Canadians pay between $200 and $300 more for a car produced in Canada than do their American neighbours for the same car after it crosses the border and is
Canada-United. States Auto Pact
purchased in Buffalo, Boston, San Francisco or any other American city.
According to a systematic study carried out recently, the four major automotive companies, General Motors, Ford, Chrysler and American Motors, charge their dealers in Canada about $250 more for a standard car produced in Canada than they charge their dealers for an identical car produced in the United States. This difference, understandably, is not absorbed by the dealers but is passed on to the Canadian consumer. After seven years of innovative restructuring of the Canadian side of the automotive industry, and I stress this, there is no excuse for this price difference.
The Canadian part of the industry is the most efficient on the North American continent. There is all kinds of evidence to show that Canadian productivity is higher than American productivity in this industry. Despite this real improvement that has occurred in our productive capacity, the Canadian consumer is not getting his due in terms of prices. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we are witnessing sheer profiteering on the part of the large companies, at the expense of the Canadian public.
I now want to talk about the safeguards and deal with them in terms of whether they are essential. The American government, a number of Canadian economists and, I suspect, even the government of Canada believe that the safeguards in the pact are no longer required. Those who take this position contend that the safeguards were merely transitional requirements needed only until parts and assembly plants in Canada could adjust to the new continental market situation. If maintained, it is said, they are simply unjust, protectionist devices which violate the intent of the pact.
The "free trade" interpreters of th e pact I suggest are simply and categorically wrong. Prior to the drafting of the pact Toronto economist, Professor V. Bladen, former head of the political economy department of the University of Toronto, had served as a one-man royal commission on the automotive industry. When so serving he cogently argued that it would be suicidal for Canada not to have safeguards in the automotive trade agreement with the United States. He said so for the obvious reason that if we give tariff free access to our market to an industry which is almost 100 per cent American owned, there would be no guarantee that Canada would get its share of future growth in the automotive industry or indeed that present Canadian production levels would be maintained. It is for this reason that the production safeguard principle was imbedded in the pact.
It is essential that we retain some such requirements in the pact, however they are formulated, which will ensure that Canada share, as the pact states, "on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total market of the two countries", or that principle is contradictory to a free trade assumption. Given the protectionist policies currently being pursued in the United States, DISC, the Burke-Hartke bill, etc., due to their own high level of unemployment, there is every reason to assume that without job-protecting safeguards in the auto pact, we would see not only a restriction in our share of the growth of the total

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact North American market to which we are entitled, but also a diminution of our present levies of production. In short, thousands of Canadian jobs are at stake.
In their discussions with Canada, the Americans have been justifiably critical of our government's failure to get automotive companies to bring their prices in Canada into line with those in the United States. One of their chief reasons for agreeing to the pact was an anticipated growth rate of 8 per cent in the Canadian automotive market for North American cars and trucks. For this to have taken place, automotive companies would have had to lower their Canadian prices. If they had done so, Canadian consumers would not be purchasing at about twice the rate of their American counterparts foreign produced automobiles and trucks.
In 1965, non-North American sales accounted for 11 per cent of the Canadian market. After six years, instead of declining, this percentage increased to 25.9 per cent for 1971, the last year for which statistics are available. In British Columbia, about 50 per cent of the cars sold are made outside North America. The percentage of such vehicles sold in the United States in 1971 was 15.8 per cent, approximately three-fifths of the Canadian level. There can be no doubt that the major reason for the significant and growing market for non-North American cars in Canada compared with that which prevails in the United States is the unwarranted overpricing which takes place in Canada.
The price gap for identical cars, after allowance was made for taxes and differing dollar value, between Canada and the United States in 1964 was approximately 9 per cent. In 1971, although there had been progress up to then, the difference was still 9 per cent. In fact, for 1972, according to one study, the price differential between cars sold in Canada and the United States, after making allowances for taxes, had increased to 10 per cent, one per cent more than it was in 1964, the year the auto pact came into being.
The four major automotive companies in Canada reap excessive profits, excessive even for an oligopoly controlled industry. According to an article published in the Globe & Mail last April 26, the per unit profit of Ford of Canada was $222 higher than the per unit profit of its United States parent. The differences for the other companies are virtually certain to be identical. The per unit profit for Ford of Canada increased in each of the four most recent years for which statistics are available. I urge the minister to note these facts. In 1968, the per unit profit was $117. That is the profit after considering all factors when the car is released through the dealer. The per unit profit for 1969 was $164; 1970, $153, and 1971, $228. I am certain the per unit profit of Chrysler and General Motors was similar.
It is interesting to note that between 1966 and 1972, the duty remissions which the companies got from the Canadian taxpayer as a result of the pact were as follows: Ford, $176,614,083; American Motors, $3,135,075; Chrysler, $1,992,607 and General Motors, $1,388,150.
It is clear that in addition to making clear the future security of Canadian automotive workers, we also need an immediate policy which will stop the gouging of Canadian consumers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 56-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 56-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
There is, I believe, a course of action which will meet the needs of both consumers and autoworkers in Canada and, incidentally, might be appealing to American opponents of the pact, whether or not they are in congress. What we propose is to remove the prohibition which compels Canadians to pay a 15 per cent duty on new cars purchased in the United States. The effect of this will be to cause the North American automotive companies to reduce the price of their cars to Canadian dealers to the level which prevails in the United States. The prospect of dealer competition in the United States will cause this reduction to be passed on to the Canadian consumer by dealers in this country. My point is if we remove the 15 per cent duty for individual consumers crossing the border, the companies in Canada will not permit their dealer systems to go under. They will stop the gouging of their own dealers which has gone on up to this point and ensure that the duty saving is transmitted into price reductions to their dealers. To stop Canadians from crossing the border into the United States to purchase their cars, the dealers in Canada will reduce their prices and the Canadian consumer will get the benefit.
However, and this is important, to ensure the preservation and growth of Canadian employment in the auto industry, production level safeguards must be maintained. Instead of basing them on consumption levels in Canada, however, changes in the automotive agreement should be proposed and negotiated by the Canadian government which would make Canadian production and CVA requirements dependent upon Canadian purchases anywhere in continental North America. A new Canadian minimum production floor level needs to be introduced for negotiation, and it should be based on 1972 levels instead of 1964 levels of production as is now the case. This approach would provide a measure of justice, long overdue, to Canadian consumers. It would also create more jobs for Canadian workers precisely because an average price reduction of $250 per car would inevitably mean that Canadians would buy more vehicles manufactured in North America and fewer imports.
To conclude, this proposal, if adopted, would mean more jobs for Canadian workers. It would also mean lower prices for Canadians. It is, then, the kind of proposal which deserves, and, I hope, will receive, the support of the party to my right and of the government which sits opposite.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 56-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
I rise to speak on this motion with some degree of admiration for the drafter; he has managed succinctly to cover the two chief areas of concern now surrounding the Canada-United States automotive trade agreement. First, he mentioned the necessity for progress under the agreement leading to the tangible mutual benefit of both countries. The key word, here, is "mutual". Second, he spoke of the continuing and worsening problem of the widening price differential between the two countries. We have little confidence in the remedy proposed by the previous speaker as solutions of these trade problems. In particular, the events of the past two weeks have shaken our confidence-and certain-

March 13, 1973

ly have shaken the confidence of the Canadian business community-in the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie).
Consider the confusing and, often, inconsistent positions and statements adopted by the government on this issue. The matter arose two weeks ago with the announcement in the United States that the Canadian automotive trade deficit with the United States was $100 million as opposed to a surplus of almost $200 million in 1971. The minister told us not to worry. Statistics Canada, he said, has set the deficit at $41 million. He said-and I am quoting: "I do not see that there is any emergency or any reason to push any panic buttons at this time." This statement is reported at page 1751 of Hansard. We agree. Nothing to panic about; there are bound to be fluctuations in our trade positions. We enjoyed surpluses in two preceding years. Now, we are faced with a relatively-and I stress the word "relatively"-small deficit by comparison with the total automobile and parts movement of nearly $7 billion annually.
Then, the minister dropped his bombshell. He referred to the paragraphs in the agreement which had traditionally been known as the Canadian safeguards as being of a transitional nature-the first time they had been described as such, to my knowledge, by a Canadian minister. Further, he said the agreement itself provided that these safeguards were transitional. The clear meaning of this statement was that the government, in a major policy shift, had adopted the United States contention that the provisions for Canadian protection in the agreement were of a short-term nature designed to get Canada over a temporary trade deficit. The implication was that they could be removed, since, as the minister further noted, they had been overfulfilled to the extent of $1 billion. We in the opposition urge that the safeguards should be maintained and, indeed, improved. If we can experience a reversal in our trading position from a surplus of $200 million to a deficit of $100 million, or whatever the correct figure is, perhaps the safeguards are inadequate.
The next day the government changed its position. The minister said he had been mistaken, that there was no mention in the agreement of the safeguards being transitional. The words were, in fact, only the words of the negotiators. That is fine. I am sure, however, that the negotiators said many things about many subjects-about free trade in used cars, about free trade at the consumer level, even about who would go out for coffee that morning. The fact remains that the agreement is a legal document with all its terms contained inside the four corners of the document itself. To accept the implications of the minister's suggestion that the words of the negotiators carry any force or effect would be totally ridiculous.
The hon. gentleman went on to assure the House that the safeguards would not be removed, but they would be improved. As reported at page 1784 of Hansard, he said, in this context:
I am certainly interested in seeing them improved, and that will be the position of the government. If there is any change with respect to these provisions it will be to improve them so as to make them more workable.
Thus, he completed the transition, if I may use that term, from implying that the safeguards might be
Canada-United States Auto Pact
dropped, to the position urged on him by members of this party that they should be improved. Then, Mr. Speaker, he had the unmitigated gall to tell the House that there is confusion in the minds of opposition questioners over this point. This was after he had gone through the process of reversing his own position twice in two days.
Again, the minister is ill-informed as to the actual terms of the agreement. The production to sales in Canada ratio, one of the protections set out in the pact, is an annual target, one which must be met each year. It is simply not open to the interpretation that it has, at some time in the past, been far exceeded and is therefore no longer a protection. The minister, as I reminded hon. members, supported the position that the safeguards were transitional by telling us that they had been over-fulfilled to the extent of $1 billion. Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as it hangs over the heads of automobile manufacturers annually to meet a certain production to sales ratio, this particular provision continues to provide protection for Canadien production and for the Canadian automobile worker.
Everyone agrees that the auto pact has been a great boon to the Canadian auto and parts manufacturing industry. We must ensure that it continues to be so. The government now admits we must attempt to improve the safeguards. Some may suggest there is little chance of our maintaining what is in the agreement now, let alone improving on it. There is no doubt the bargaining sessions are going to be tough, and it may well be that in order to gain trading concessions or improvements we shall have to give ground in other areas. It may well be that the auto pact requires some amendment.
Obviously, the Americans think the safeguards are an extremely important factor in the reversal of their trade fortunes in this area. They have been pressing strongly for changes during the last four or five years. This being the case, we have a strong bargaining lever at our disposal, one which could well be used to bring us better safeguards. Surely, though, it is a fundamental bargaining principle not to show one's hand or reveal what one is prepared to give up prior to the commencement of the bargaining sessions. In other words, one should not give away gratis in the House of Commons what is a significant bargaining lever which could be used to gain other concessions at the bargaining table. The stumbling and fumbling of the minister on the whole matter over the past few weeks inspires little confidence in us, and, more importantly, little confidence in the Canadian manufacturing sector of our economy.
As I said at the start, the words "mutual benefit of both countries" in this motion are the key. We feel that the future negotiations with the United States should be directed towards working out a set of mutual safeguards which will protect automobile production and jobs in both countries.
The point that perhaps most raises the hackles of the United States is the fact that the present safeguards are designed chiefly to ensure a fair share of auto production and jobs to Canada. I hold no brief for the United States. They are certainly able to take care of themselves at the bargaining table. But if the present protections continue

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact to result in a widening balance in favour of Canada, we cannot complain too vociferously about some means of controlling such a situation. In this respect, let us keep in mind that this was not the case during this past year. Canada suffered a setback in her over-all trade balance of nearly $200 million, but the prior two years had resulted in automobile trade surpluses in our favour of a substantial amount in each case.
Measures of mutual benefit could include-and I say could-an agreement, for example, or a term in an amended auto pact agreement, to relate employment in the industry to the consumption of cars and parts in both countries. For instance, if Canada consumes 13 per cent of the North American market, we should reasonably expect to enjoy 13 per cent of the production facilities, capital expenditures and, of course, jobs.
Alternatively, as another example of the type of term that might well provide mutual protection for both Canada and the United States, the agreement could be amended to provide a floor and a ceiling for the Canadian value added requirements; or, upper and lower surplus and deficit limits which in both cases, if reached, would trigger penalty mechanisms and the imposition of duties to encourage companies to reverse the undesirable trend.
I am being deliberately vague, Mr. Speaker, because I subscribe to the view of the minister-I know we do not agree on too many things, but on this point I do agree- that bargaining in public is not a desirable or profitable practice. Perhaps the minister should have followed his own advice when he suggested two weeks ago that the safeguards were of a transitional nature. Suffice it to say that there are very positive steps that can be taken in the interests of both countries to overcome these irritants which have grown up and now exist between us with respect to this agreement.
The motion before the House urges the government to take certain steps to lower the prices of automobiles to Canadian consumers and to protect the jobs of Canadian auto workers. The agreement itself has adequately, even admirably, protected jobs in Canada over the course of its duration. The agreement, however, does not specifically dictate the price of cars or require any type of movement toward parity of prices between the two countries. Presumably it was thought that with a free market at the manufacturing level there would be a gradual movement toward price parity; and in fact this has been the case, or was the case for the first few years of the agreement. However, as the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) has pointed out, this is not the case at present. In fact, in the past year the situation has worsened and this is an area of major concern. The price gap in 1972 actually widened from what it was in 1971.
I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to the sixth annual report of the President of the United States to Congress on the operation of the auto pact. This report, not yet available to the public, will be released shortly and contains some disturbing facts and figures. The document, albeit a United States-biased review of the situation, contains figures that show that both the wholesale and retail price differentials on selected, typical cars widened instead of narrowed in 1972. For instance, on a typical 4-door, 6-cylinder sedan with comparable equipment, the

wholesale price was 10.8 per cent higher in Canada than in the U.S. in 1972. This is an icnrease from 10.6 per cent in 1971, but more significantly the 1971 figure was down from a 14.2 per cent difference in 1970, and an 18.5 per cent difference in 1965. As a second example, on a typical 4-door, 8-cylinder sedan with standard equipment, the wholesale price difference jumped in 1972 to 10.9 per cent, up from 9.9 per cent in 1971, but again down from the 1970 figure of 13.9 per cent and the 1965 figure of 18.5 per cent.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, the disturbing element of these figures is the fact that the trend from 1965, which continued through the end of 1971, reversed itself in 1972. The reversals and differences are marginal, but the interruption of the trend is significant and unfortunate to the Canadian position. On some more expensive models the trend has not been interrupted, but the facts very clearly show that on the lower and medium priced cars, the models which the average consumers in Canada purchase, there exists a continuing high difference in car prices between our two countries. And, more significantly, this differential is not narrowing. This in spite of the fact that it has been this government's stated aim over a number of years to narrow this difference.
Despite this policy and these pessimistic figures, this government failed to dissuade the automobile manufacturers from increasing prices in 1973. Again, the government knows the tools and persuasive devices available to it to put some muscle into its requests of the companies that they reduce or limit further increases in prices. However, it simply lacks the resolve or the ability to do other than pay lip service to the narrowing of the price gap.
A further significant, and again upsetting, feature of this report of this very concise analysis of the auto pact agreement is the number of references to the safeguards as being of a transitional nature. This may be a sidelight or tip-off, but it is interesting to note that the word "transitional" is used in this report prepared for the President of the United States-it is a very short report consisting of some 26 pages-a total of eight times, almost to the point of it being taken for granted, at least by United States officials, that the safeguards were in fact transitional.
However, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member's motion is correct. The government has failed to develop a policy that would benefit Canadians and resolve the conflicts concerning the Canada-United States automotive agreement. It is also obvious that the government cannot be relied upon to come up with solutions, despite the proposals included in this motion. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) yesterday refused to review the government's long-term objectives under the auto pact, if indeed they have long-term or even shortterm objectives at all. At least to date, they have failed to make any comments in this respect.
What is more important, however, is that this motion will permit the government to continue on this path. The government have proved that they will not or cannot solve the problem. For this reason we feel the motion should have been one of non-confidence. If the motion is an accurate expression of the NDP attitude toward the government's position on this matter I fail to see, and our party fails to see, how they could harbour any confidence in the government whatsoever in this respect. It is unfor-
March 13, 1973

tunate that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and his NDP caucus did not make this a vote confidence.

speechtext: It is not forbidden. It is unfortunate that they have sacrificed one more issue for the survival of this government. It is unfortunate that they did not think to move to censure the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), since that would have allowed them to remain true to their convictions rather than the government as a whole as they have been for the past three months.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 56-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first to congratulate hon. members of the New Democratic Party on a motion that reads in part as follows:
... to lower the prices of automobiles to Canadian consumers and to protect the jobs of Canadian autoworkers.
All sorts of arguments are put forward on this subject, to prove that the auto pact is to the advantage of Canadians or to that of the Americans.
One hears discussion about profits, and unfortunately, each of the countries in turn seems to justify its position with regard to the pact by saying that it has made a profit and that the agreement has been to its advantage.
And so, if both countries have built up surpluses, one wonders what changes can be made, since that would seem to be the real solution to both countries' problems.
However, even if Canada declares a surplus of $5,800,000, and at the same time the United States declares a surplus of $38 million, there is no changing the fact that the auto pact is still no more than a way of promoting American products, whether or not some of them are made in Canada. It still remains that we are working to benefit American companies such as Chrysler, GM, Ford and American Motors, because their Canadian branches are still integral parts of the parent establishments, which are American companies.
I cannot find in the Canada-U.S.A. auto pact or in the current debate-whether it be the arguments put forward by the NDP, the Progressive Conservative party or the past achievements of the Liberal party-not one suggestion as to how to create an essentially Canadian car industry.
In Quebec we have had the experience of a corporation which tried to manufacture a Canadian car. We have had the example of the Manic corporation which went bankrupt for lack of assistance or interest from the provincial or federal governments. In the meantime, we are still trying to negotiate agreements between American and Canadians for manufacturing American cars.
Canadians should not be sold a bill of goods: Canadian cars and parts will be made by subsidiaries of American companies which in most cases market only one model of the American series. Let us take for instance the Biscayne of the General Motors of Canada which is the only American model manufactured in Canada. But what is done to manufacture a typically Canadian vehicle?
Canada-United States Auto Pact
I will go even further than that. When it comes to the manufacturing standards of those companies serious problems arise. For instance, it can be seen that the Americans do not care about the Canadian market when they turn out windshield wipers designed to slip under the hood; this may be quite convenient in the United States but not at all in Canada because of our climate.
The United States control both manufacturing and standards so that we have little elbow room and accept that control and those standards, thereby creating problems for ourselves as we do not manufacture a typically Canadian product made expressly for the [DOT] Canadian climate.
We have discussed and are still discussing those problems without ever really encouraging the creation of a typically Canadian industry. I suppose the Canada-United States auto pact was beneficial to Canada, but we notice that when American companies wished to start production in Canada, it was because they wanted to get cheap labour although Canadians realized every year that through pressure or union militancy we could get salaries comparable with those of the Americans.
But although we manage to achieve near wage partity and a balance in the exchange of automobile parts with the United States, we realize that it is always to the detriment of the creation of a typically Canadian industry.
For instance since 1965, it is true that we gained some advantage from that agreement. As a matter of fact, it is said that the pact created 100,000 new jobs. But if the government in 1965 had promoted the creation of a typically Canadian industry, those 100,000 jobs would have been created just the same, but the industry would have been under Canadian and not American control.
That is what should be done; it is not a matter of protectionist measures, of some anti-American attitude, but of a pro-Canadian attitude in the industrial field. The Canada-United States auto pact is but one example of it.
One realizes that snowmobiles are also involved. The Bombardier Company Limited has laid off 125 employees because 50,000 of its snowmobiles remained unsold. One realizes also that importing those snowmobiles, as the U.S. Trade Department puts it, causes some problem:
Snowmobile imports from Canada, according to the Department, rose from $22 million in 1971 to $33 million last year, whereas snowmobile imports from the U.S. fell from $124 million to $104 million.
There again, comparisons can be made concerning a really beneficial production for Canadians. Of course, the idea is to lessen the cost of automobiles for the Canadian people, but, then again, I do not believe that we may reach that goal through bargaining with the United States or through administrative measures laid down by the federal government.
Therefore, why not subsidize the purchase of those cars or provide assistance to consumers themselves in Canada? What is the purpose of the government trying to enter into agreements with the large corporations? Why not create a compensated discount system applying to products made in Canada. Such a compensated discount system would bring about a solution allowing reduction of

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact
the cost of cars, and the creation of a Canadian auto industry whose production would be protected.
This point is not brought forward in the Canada-United States auto pact as there is no intention of touching upon that point, though it would represent a valuable protectionist solution applying to the jobs and markets in Canada.
There again, it is noted that the United States speak out. In fact,the Washington Post states plainly that Canada, on account of those consultations or phony talks, if I may say so, between corporations and the government, we are increasingly importing unemployment from the United States to Canada because the United States want to protect their market, their production. Then, we get involved in their arguments and let ourselves be dragged hither and thither and-I always come back to that-without trying to set up our own automobile industry.
They say:
... many Canadians are afraid that the United States government is determined to intensify the employment rate in American plants, even at the cost of corresponding unemployment in Canadian plants . ..
