speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry. Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to start off by saying that I listened very closely to the comments of the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Caouette) with respect to the automobile industry in Canada, as well as some of his suggestions with respect to how we might go about developing a distinctive Canadian automobile industry in Canada. I noted as well the fact that he spoke about the snowmobile as a peculiarly successful Canadian invention, something which, incidentally-and perhaps not all members are aware of it-enters into the United States duty free under the provisions of the automotive pact.
During the course of my remarks I hope to be able to comment on some of the criticisms and suggestions of the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whit-by (Mr. Broadbent) and of the hon. member for Halton (Mr. O'Connor). But first, I think it might be profitable, because this is an important occasion when we are dealing with the auto pact, to review some of the circumstances which gave birth to the auto pact and to trace its history, and then move into the situation which we are at present considering.
March 13, 1973

I think it might be worthwhile to remember that in the early 1960's there was considerable concern in Canada about the substantial current account trade deficit with respect to automobiles and with respect to the efficiency of our Canadian automobile industry. Higher costs were associated with short-run assembly and manufacturing operations. There was duty payable on imported parts, and the costs of writing-off tooling and facilities was on a much smaller volume. All of this added to the higher unit cost in Canada. The proliferation of styles, because each automobile manufacturer was tending to produce the full stable of cars on both sides of the border, again added to the unit costs and to prices in Canada. Considering all these factors-the balance of payments factor, the unit cost factor, and the need to develop a new strategy for the automobile industry-the government put together a plan which it put to the United States government. This plan was based on rationalizing the North American market and was designed to provide for the mutual benefit of both countries in the sense of increasing the size of the market for the North American made vehicle, a plan which would provide for a more efficient Canadian manufacturing industry and lower costs to the Canadian consumer.
These particular objectives are reflected in the automotive agreement. I think one can say that without doubt the agreement is one of the most imaginative, and certainly one of the most important trading arrangements ever made between our two countries. The agreement recognized, and I quote:
The important place that the automotive industry occupies in the industrial economy of the two countries and the interests of industry, labour and consumers in sustaining high levels of efficient production and continued growth in the automotive industry.
It is designed to achieve a substantial expansion in production and employment, and to promote improved competitive efficiency in the automotive industries in both countries. Three fundamental objectives are set out in Article I of the agreement. The first is the creation of a broader market for automotive products within which full benefits of specialization and large scale production can be achieved. The second is the liberalization of the U.S.A. and Canadian automotive trade in respect of trade barriers and other factors tending to impede it, with a view to enabling industries of both countries to participate on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total markets in both countries. The third is the development of conditions in which market forces may operate effectively to obtain the most economic pattern of investment, production and trade.
The hon. member for Halton challenged me to say what are the long-term objectives of the auto pact. From the point of view of this government they are the same as they were when the agreement was first signed. They are those which I have put forward again just within the last few minutes. They are the expansion of the market for the North American made vehicle, the participation in that expanded market by Canadian producers and employees generally, and thirdly an efficient Canadian manufacturing industry because, and I think this is worth underlining, only through a highly efficient, highly competitive
Canada-United. States Auto Pact
Canadian manufacturing industry in the automotive area are we going to obtain the real assurances that we seek of being able to share in the benefits of the automotive agreement.
May I now turn to the question of how do we stack up in meeting these objectives. What has the government done to meet these objectives? In recognition of the differences in size, financial strength, and the relative development of our industries, special provisions were established to ensure that Canada, in fact as well as in theory, would derive real and reciprocal benefits on a fair and equitable basis. Moreover, it was recognized that it is necessary to take into account the institutional barriers to trade, arising out of the corporate structure of the industry, as well as the formal governmental barriers, if Canadian industries are to be able to participate effectively in the United States market.
Another important feature, and here I quote from the then Minister of Industry's statement to the House on May 5, 1966, was "the acceptance of the principle that Canadian industry is entitled to a reasonable transitional period to facilitate its adaptation to production for the larger international market." Furthermore, the agreement placed the automotive program on an agreed basis, thereby giving companies in both countries reasonable assurance about its permanence and status.
To take advantage of the new market opportunities provided by the program, the government instituted financial assistance to companies to expand and modernize their facilities and to assist workers. I will deal with those particular programs in a moment, but first I would like to review in statistical terms the indication of success for the pact. Some of these figures have already been given by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. He has referred to the quite striking development, the advance in direct employment.
I emphasize that total direct employment in Canada's automotive industry has risen by 41 per cent, from just under 70,000 employees employed directly in automotive plants and by component manufacturers, to just under 100,000 in 1972 which, as I say, is an increase of 41 per cent from 1964 to 1972. This does not include all the indirect employment that has been associated with that type of activity. You can choose your own multiplier, Mr. Speaker. That multiplier may go from one to three, but the fact is that some multiplier of that 28,000 to 30,000 direct employee increase has resulted from the success of the automotive agreement.
I think that we should also emphasize the basic parity, the income factor, in addition to the number of jobs that have resulted from the automotive agreement. I think it is worth underlining that during the period of the agreement from 1964 to 1972 there has been a very significant increase in the wage levels of Canadian employees in these factories, up to a point of basic parity. This does not mean that in every instance Canadian automobile workers are paid the same as United States automobile workers, but the wages are very close. I am told that in some Canadian plants the workers are now being paid more, so that the total income increase for employees has been very much larger than the 41 per cent I indicated a moment ago. On the production side, because of the

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact
rationalization of the industry, there has been a very marked increase, from something like 671,000 vehicles in this country in 1964 to 1.5 million vehicles this past year. And our increase in trade with the United States in automotive products, as a result of the agreement, has been tremendous.
The hon. member for Halton noted our balance of trade. I do not think that we should judge the success of the agreement in terms of the trade balance between our two countries. I think we should look at it in terms of the total increase in trade. When the automotive agreement was started in 1964 the total two-way trade was of the order of about $800 million, made up of something under $100 million of exports from Canada to the United States, and close to $700 million from the United States to Canada. What was it last year? Last year the total trade, two way trade between our two nations, was $9.2 billion an increase of over ten times in that period of eight years.
Mr. Speaker, with respect to the trade balance figures that I alluded to a moment ago, I think that the trade balance, in terms of surplus or deficit between our two nations, will fluctuate from time to time. The important point to underline is that we were in a significant deficit position in 1964, a $600 million deficit position. As a result of the automotive agreement, we have increased our sales and reduced that deficit so that we are now in a very small surplus position on trade account. If we include the invisible items, the non-merchandise items, you would find that Canada is still in deficit on a bilateral basis with the United States.
I think I should also point out that we are in deficit as a nation, in imports over exports, with the rest of the trading world in automobiles. This is one reason that I, for one, am anxious to see the agreement work in Canada so that we can expand the market for the North American made vehicle, which is something that I believe all hon. members would like to see.
Let me now touch on some of the measures to which reference has been made. I mentioned earlier production and employment which have substantially increased in Canada since the agreement was signed. Indeed, the value of production has increased by more than one billion dollars over the minimum production requirement in the agreement-the Canadian value added so-called safeguard. These requirements therefore, because they are one billion dollars over the level prescribed in the agreement, have no real or safeguarding relevance to present levels of production and employment in Canada. That was the point I was trying to make the other day, Mr. Speaker, when I was questioned on this in this House.
The growth in the industry in Canada has been assisted by three programs, as I have mentioned. The first, the adjustment assistance program, was designed to assist Canadian parts manufacturers through this transitional period that I have referred to earlier. To date, it has made 114 loans amounting to approximately $100 million and additional applications are being processed. Second, a transitional financial assistance program for workers was also established to assist in the adjustment process. Only a relatively small number of workers found it necessary 
to take part in this program because of the relative buoyancy of the automotive market. Third, the government introduced a special remission program on production machinery required by the industry to take full advantage of the expanding opportunities. This program was designed to ensure that vehicle and parts manufacturers obtained machinery and equipment on a competitive basis with the industry in the United States.
At the time of the agreement the then minister of industry, Mr. Drury, stated:
In line with the attainment of lower costs of production, it is anticipated, as the program develops, that the forces of competition will gradually result in savings to the Canadian consumer in the form of a narrowing differential between the Canadian and United States prices for motor vehicles and components.
I should like now to touch on that important question of prices and I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if you could indicate to me how much time I have left.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I have another ten minutes, so I shall talk about prices. There has been much discussion regarding car prices in Canada and the differential that exists between the factory price of a vehicle delivered to a Canadian dealer and the factory price of a vehicle delivered to a United States dealer. This, I believe, is the important level at which we should assess the price because this is the level where the differential can be controlled.
Hon. members are aware that there are other levels, particularly the dealer level at which the consumer buys the automobile. I think comparisons are difficult because in Canada we have a federal sales tax of 12 per cent and there is no such sales tax in the United States. Also, whenever the comparison is made the provincial sales tax must be added to the end price and compared with whatever sales tax there might be in the United States. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, the comparison should be made at the factory level and I believe hon. members would agree with that.
When the automotive agreement was signed, the differential between factory level prices in Canada and the United States was of the order of 17 per cent. Regardless of the fluctuations and the effect of the exchange rate between then and now the differential is of the order of 8.5 per cent to 9 per cent. In other words, the price differential during the course of the agreement has declined by one half between '64 and '72. You can also put it the other way around: Canadian car prices over this period have risen only half as fast as car prices in the United States. This price gap varies from company to company and model to model. What we are talking about here are weighted averages of the whole piece.
The hon. member for Halton read some information into the record which I gather he regards as private or confidential or not accessible to the general public. To me, it seemed to be based on a model to model comparison rather than a weighted average of all models in all parts of the country. But the comparison, for purposes of rating
March 13, 1973

the differential, has to be on an average across the piece on a company by company basis. Hon. members from the west coast may know that some Canadian automobiles are priced so competitively that they are even less expensive than similar models across the border in the Pacific coast market. Most, however, are more expensive by varying amounts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure the hon. member that I have not overlooked his interesting suggestions. I will comment on them in my concluding remarks, soon to be made.
I emphasize that not only from the point of view of fairness to the consumer is the lowering of the price differential important; it is important, as well, from the point of view of the security and growth of the pact itself, because the lower the Canadian car price is relative to the price of the foreign imported or foreign made car, the greater will be the market for the North American made vehicle in North America and the greater will be the participation of Canadians in that market. That is why, within days of being appointed Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I moved directly to deal with this question. I talked to the automobile manufacturers. Within a week of my appointment, I took action, and as I said the result of that action was that which I have already announced to the House, namely, the price freeze with respect to the 1973 model year. This will be imposed here regardless of any increase that may be imposed in the United States. There is a further undertaking on the part of the companies with respect to narrowing the price differential in the present and in the 1974 model year.
Some hon. members have alluded to various voices in the United States indicating that the agreement should be changed in some particular. I listened carefully to the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and the hon. member for Charlevoix. I wanted to hear their suggestions and hear any guidance they might offer with respect to what changes, if any, might, in their view, be beneficial for this country. I have indicated in my remarks in the House during the question period that we have taken no decision to change the agreement. There has been no change in the agreement. I repeat, we have taken no decision to change it, for one good reason: in our view, the agreement is working to the mutual benefit of both countries and it is working very well.
It may be that we should consider changes in the agreement. It may be that we might be able to contemplate changes which would be to the mutual benefit of both parties to the agreement. I should like to reassure the House about the statement I made on March 1. If there is any change in the provisions of the automotive agreement, it should be to improve them so as to make them more workable. Although I do not foresee any imminent changes in the present agreement, I want to assure the House again that if changes are made, they will be made in accordance with the objectives of that agreement, and with the proviso that they are to the mutual benefit of both countries. That means that they could not be to the disadvantage of Canada and still be acceptable to this government.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to assure the House once more that the effort of this government will be to continue to provide for the future expansion of automobile production and to secure future job opportunities for Canadians in our automotive industry. While I can appreciate to some extent the concern that motivated the bringing of the motion now before us, I suggest that it should be readily apparent to members of all parties that no Canadian government, of whatever stripe, could con-

I know there exists a 12 per cent excise tax on Canadian cars and similar American taxes have been removed, but I do not think we should deal with that today because it is not the central issue in this debate. The auto purchaser in my part of the country is seldom told that he is currently paying to the hilt for his car because our friendly American subsidiaries which build his Canadian automobile are pocketing over $150 million of his hard earned money each year. They are charging him 10 per cent extra because he is a Canadian and his government lets them get away with it. That is what I would like the people of British Columbia to know and the people in the rest of Canada as well.
When I mentioned to some of my B.C. friends that I intended to speak in this debate today, they just smiled and said for all the interest I would create in my riding, I might as well make a speech about wheat. I will leave that for the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight). It is assumed that most people do not really care about the end price of a car. All that really interests the average guy is whether he can scrape up the downpayment and hack the carrying charges of $95 a month or so. I am not persuaded, however, that this simplistic notion is accurate. If it were so, why would half the people in British Columbia be buying the offshore imports such as Datsun, Toyota, Volkswagens and Renaults? I think that B.C. people buy these cars because they are cheaper. It is as simple as that. They buy Datsuns, Toyotas, Volkswagens and Renaults in a greater proportion than they buy Gremlins, Vegas and Pintos because offshore imports are cheaper. However, these offshore car manufacturers do not employ a single Canadian worker while American subsidiaries operating in Canada, according to the minister's figures, employ nearly 100,000.
The debate today does not really have anything to do with the car culture of North America. We could say a great deal about the problems of disruption and changes over 50 years of North American automania. We are not going to discuss the land-gobbling freeways, carnage on the highways, the pollution befouled cities or the urban sprawl created by any combination of these things. However, all these in themselves are worthy of serious debate at another time.
We must remind ourselves today in dealing with the motion put forward by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), and the new suggestions that flow from it, that Canadians consume or are consumed by a certain number of cars per year. Despite the auto pact, these built-in-Canada cars are vastly overpriced. Because of the overpricing, foreign imports are stealing an ever-increasing share of the Canadian market, thus reducing or not expanding job opportunities proportionately for Canadian workers. These concerns are legitimate enough at any time, but in the current unemployment-inflation environment in which we now find ourselves today, to continue blindly along the same old paths is not only unacceptable but intolerable.
In case the proposals of my colleague have not been made clear to the minister, members opposite or any other member who might have tuned in late, let me repeat them. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby suggested
25789-65)
Canada-United, States Auto Pact
first, the removal of the 15 per cent duty on North American cars purchased in the United States to, in effect, push the Canadian subsidiaries into lowering their prices to United States levels in order to protect their dealers in Canada. The second point was to maintain the principle of safeguards, but to change their content so that Canadian purchases of North American automobiles anywhere in North America would be counted in the production-consumption figures. The third point was to amend the floor level below which Canadian production could not fall from the base output in 1964 to a new base of 1972 production-consumption.
I shall not attempt to expand on the reasons for these proposals in any great detail because I think the hon. member has ably done that. What I intend to do in the time remaining to me is to examine the verbalized, if not sincere concern for the consumer in this day of consumerism and how the price differential of about $300 is a felony compounded by a spin-off of added costs far greater than the $300 differential.
As an example, I will use an intermediate sized car, the Chevelle Malibu 8, two door, with a 307-v8 engine aboard. The 1973 list price or windshield sticker for this car f.o.b. Oshawa, using rounded figures for clarity, with no attempt at obscurity or obfuscation, is $3,300. On a clean deal, with no trade in, this car would probably be sold to a customer for about $3,000. Again using the ball park figure, its price in Seattle would be roughly $2,700, the dealer mark up being about the same in percentage terms. The $300 price differential is punitive enough, but let us consider what the extra $300 over the American price does in car financing.
Assuming that a customer pays $1,000 down and proposes to finance the remaining $2,000 through GMAC at roughly 16 per cent, the finance charges are approximately $409. The same plan to finance a car $300 less expensive would provide a $150 saving on financing, a considerable saving to anyone. We all know that the poor seldom have $1,000 to put down on a car and, therefore, the financing is usually carried on a larger amount, say $2,500, and over a longer period of time, say 36 months. I have these figures, but I think the figures which are quoted in any speech will show similar dramatic differences. Of course, more affluent Canadians can usually avoid finance companies and seek much lower interest rates through banks or credit unions, but those with poor credit often have no alternative but to go for higher interest rates. The less affluent pay much more for their financing for cars or anything else.
Let us add the cost of insuring the automobile with the $300 larger price. I do not say larger value because value is not always reflected in the price charged. I was reliably informed this morning that the difference in the competitive Ontario insurance market, we anticipate public auto insurance in British Columbia, is $15 per year or $30 over the two year financing period I am using in my example. Auto parts, new fenders and auto glass are similarly going to be 10 per cent higher, but I cannot include these in the extra burden of the $300 overcharge because I have no way to estimate their influence. I do not know whether the car will run into difficulty or whether it will be involved in

March 13, 1973
Canada-United. States Auto Pact
an accident. These extra costs nevertheless cannot help but be a burden on the consumer.
Let us add the 24 month package of extra costs associated with car purchasing in Canada under fairly common financing terms. The extra cost to the Canadian car purchaser is $300. The extra financing of the $300 is $150. The extra insurance cost is $30. This adds up to $480. This is the extra penalty against the Canadian car purchaser which I insist is unjust, unreasonable and unacceptable. Perhaps Mr. Speaker, I have made the point that the difference is not just $300, but the financing, the insurance and the cost of parts magnify and distort the real differences which perhaps are hidden. These costs are directed to the Canadian consumer, not to this benefit but for the sole purpose of giving a $150 million bonanza each year to our friendly American subsidiaries.
Before I sit down I should like to touch upon a couple of other points. First, I think in addition to the three proposals articulated earlier by my hon. friend, we should consider the implications of dutyless access to used cars as well as new ones. To avoid the shock which would occur to Canadian retailers who might suffer because western Canadians at least might seek year-old cars in the say, California market, perhaps we could phase in the used car policy gradually over, a five-year period. We should, I repeat, study access to used cars and do our best to mitigate any injury which Canadian dealers might face. I am asking hon. members to consider the implications. That is all I am going to do at the moment. But isn't the point here that lower prices would come to the consumer? If we are interested in the cost of living problem, that is one thing we should consider.
The second point I should like to mention is that, as a British Columbian, I see no reason why all Canadian car plants, except for the one in Halifax, are located in central Canada. Everyone knows that there is a sizeable automobile industry in California and there could be an auto assembly plant in B.C. as well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
In western Canada we are far too dependent on the primary industries, capital intensive ones, and we do not nearly approach a balance of the secondary, labour-intensive industries of which the auto industry is a part. It should be pointed out that White Trucks, for instance, through a DREE grant, I think, located an assembly plant in Kelowna, British Columbia, and similar auto assembly plants, regardless of country of origin would be welcome in British Columbia.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in pre-auto pact days, a fairly large segment of the population which was interested in such things, looked at the little country of Sweden and said, how can the Swedes produce the Volvo and yet Canada has no truly Canadian car? Should we be manufacturing an all-Canadian car? There was a suggestion

that this car should be called the Beaver, or something like that. A lot of people had some gnawing doubts about the Beaver, but I predict that if we do not resolve our present difficulties to the mutual benefit of the two countries involved in this auto pact there will be a hue and cry for reconsideration of the Beaver. An indigenous Canadian car is, perhaps, an unrealistic and presumably unnecessary concept provided we can negotiate in good faith, basing our negotiations-and I like the suggestion of the hon. member for Halton-on a policy in which we can have confidence. I suggest the three proposals of my hon. friend from Oshawa-Whitby might provide a very good basis from which to begin.
The purchase of an automobile is the most important and largest purchase the Canadian family makes. But people don't make it once or twice or three times in a lifetime, like their homes; they make these purchases every three or four years. So, I am urging the minister, and suggesting to him for the sake of nearly every Canadian family, for the sake of the cost of living, for the sake of the spin-off of the differential and the added financial burden because of this spin-off of the added cost he has to face, that the average Canadian consumer of automobiles would be most grateful to the minister if he used one of his great assets, his great persuasive ability. When next he goes, into the negotiations, the minister should go with determination to end this price differential, and the best way to do that in my opinion is get rid of the protective 15 percent tariff. If this were done, the Canadian consumer, not just the Canadian producer, could benefit by applying continentalism to the automobile market in North America.

It is interesting that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) in his motion should have laid the blame for the auto pact on the Liberal government. Yet here is a pact which he is trying to preserve, and rightly so. I do not really understand why he suggests there should be blame. Of course, there should be a great deal of credit, and a great deal of credit goes to men like the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) who is with us here, now.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
There is nobody in this House who consistently, in or out of politics, has taken a firmer position for Canada. He has been a credit to Canada. He knows how to deal toughly, also fairly, and has always consistently sought to do those things which would be best for this country economically, culturally and even spiritually. I say this without being facetious. I remember one of his early speeches in the House of Commons when he came here as a new member. He spoke about maintaining and preserving the spirit of Canada, the culture of Canada, the whole flavour of our Canadian mosaic. So no one else could better bargain on our behalf. He will do it seriously, he will do it toughly, he will do it practically and he will do
March 13, 1973

it fairly. Being fair is half the battle. He, like myself, came here from the private sector of business and there is nothing that works in the long run if it is not fair and to the advantage of both parties involved. Political posturing is unproductive. Showing how tough we can be may get us shorter term gains but over-toughness or unfairness or unreasonableness or stupidity is long remembered. We could win battles and we could lose wars.
What are our objectives under the automotive trade agreement? I look back on those years. I remember them well. In 1964, when this pact was negotiated, the Canadian car market accounted for 7.5 per cent of the North American market and we only produced some 4 per cent. We ran a $600 million deficit annually. There were two general objectives. One was to correct this imbalance and the other was to correct the price differential. The latter has yet to be achieved. The differential at that time was some 17 per cent, if I recall correctly and today it is something like 8.5 per cent; it is coming down. The minister has fought hard for this since the day he took over his present portfolio. I think we all stand firmly behind him.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, on the suggestion regarding allowing United States vehicles into Canada duty free, made a very helpful and interesting contribution, one that I looked at with interest and which I discussed with the Americans in the last Canada-U.S. interparliamentary group meeting. However, I hope it does not come to using blackmail against Canadian automobile manufacturers. I think that if Canadian manufacturers and parent companies are made aware that we are prepared to be tough and that any measures put through the House by the minister to make certain that prices are brought down to a more reasonable level will be backed not only by members on this side but, I am certain, by members on the other side of the House, I am sure we shall achieve our objective.
After all these years we now have roughly $9 billion worth of trade in automotive products. I believe the minister said this was split about 50-50 each way. How close it is to 50 is sometimes a difficult matter for us to determine since our statistics are different. We have the vice-president of General Motors in the States talking on February 28 about a surplus of $100 million; then on March 5 the Globe and Mail speaks of a $35 million surplus, both of these figures in favour of the United States; then the next day the Canadian Press reports a $38 million surplus.
As far as Statistics Canada is concerned, they have three sets of figures: firstly, a $100 million deficit in favour of the United States; then a $41 million deficit; and finally there is a $5.8 million surplus in Canada's favour. Surely there is something wrong here that needs to be corrected. When we are talking about a subject as massive and important as the auto pact we ought to have our arithmetic right.
I suggest that an important part of any renegotiation with the United States would be the development of a statistical centre so that we would be able to compare apples with apples. If we could devise some such system of reporting and maintaining statistics in a computerized fashion, where we would both have the same figures, then
Canada-United States Auto Pact
even if we differed at least we would know why we differed. Certainly that is not the case now.
What has happened during the period between 1964 and today? We produced 671,018 vehicles in Canada in 1964. By 1972, the latest figures I have, we were producing 1,472,547 vehicles, an increase of 120 per cent. The employment statistics are rather interesting. My figures only go to 1971, but in 1964 some 69,000 people were employed in the automotive industry. By 1971 this number had risen to 91,900, an increase of 32 per cent. I think the most recent figure is 97,000 for 1972, but I am a little behind in my research here. The point is that we are talking of an increase in employment in the 32 to 35 per cent range, and an increase in production of 120 per cent.
We would like to know what accounts for this. It may be greater Canadian productivity. I am sure part of it is that we have become more efficient. How much of it is due to economies of scale? In my personal dealings with the automotive industry I have seen plants which were on short runs bringing in automotive parts from the United States at high cost or from other Canadian plants at uneconomic cost. These plants were working below optimum efficiency. As hon. members know, optimum efficiency is one of the objectives of the automotive trade agreement. How much is lack of labour intensity? How much is due to sophisticated methods that require labour to be siphoned off, with an equivalent increase in the U.S. labour market?
These are the kind of matters we must look at, Mr. Speaker. I hope it is all a question of increased efficiency, economies of scale and better Canadian productivity. I think we should look at the mix of the figures of 120 per cent increased productivity and 32 to 35 per cent increased employment. In any event, it demonstrates through the great eloquence of statistics that the agreement is not stealing jobs from American workers, certainly not in proportion to the benefit that each country derives from the automotive agreement.
We talk of safegurards in the agreement and it has almost become a bad word to use. It is a sort of four-letter word in this context. The word "transitional" has also become a little distorted. Hon. members will recall that the initial safeguards were a dollar figure of $780 million in Canadian value added, a figure passed long ago and which is now up to $2 billion. The only safeguard here is the health of the industry and the achievement of our objectives. These safeguards were minimums, and mini-mums must still apply. But the word itself has become symbolic and we are hung up about it. It is highly sensitive, politically, in both countries. The real safeguard, however, must be that of balanced production, of equivalent production for equivalent markets in both countries.
When we come to negotiate with our friends to the south, we may get into difficulty because they will tell us that this year we have had a surplus. For the first six or seven years we had a deficit; then for two years we had a surplus, and we might have another this year. Surely to goodness they ought to realize that in a scheme of this magnitude fluctuations must take place which can distort very considerably the picture in a market as small as Canada's, even more than is the case in the United States.

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact
For example, there was the market decision taken by Ford to produce a small, compact car called the Maverick, built at Talbotville, near St. Thomas, Ontario. Because of that market decision, a production decision followed. Due to the fact that the plant in Canada was on stream, producing well and accepted that market decision, we made tremendous sales through that plant and thus a distortion in that year was created. I remember speaking to our American counterparts about this matter when we were discussing this agreement in Ottawa in 1970.
Even in the sale of snowmobiles distortions arise. If you lumped the sales of snowmobiles together and made them a separate item, you would find that the exports of snowmobiles in 1971 amounted to the total surplus in Canada's favour. In 1971, exports of snowmobiles amounted to $138.9 million. But what happened this year? Sales are down to $116.1 million. What has happened is that the marketing pipeline for snowmobiles has been filled. People have a first and a second snowmobile now, so are not buying them so quickly.
In addition to this, due to the success of the Bombardier snowmobile, built at Valcourt in Quebec, which really gave these sales impetus, United States manufacturers followed suit and now have their own snowmobile industry which is creating competition for Canadian snowmobiles. They exported snowmobiles to Canada in 1971 to the tune of $33.9 million, and in 1972 to the amount of $52.2 million. So, again, distortions are appearing. I think it is terribly unfair of good trading partners to take a one or two year period out of context. That is extremely important.
There have been other benefits to United States industry, the United States economy and the U.S. government. I speak of the balance of payments picture, to which the minister referred. From my own private experience in the machinery business I know one plant in Richmond, Indiana, which Senator Hartke represents, from which we imported several million dollars worth of machinery for the production of automotive parts. A lot of these machines went to the General Motors plant in Oshawa which is in the constituency of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby.
There are also management fees which go back to the United States. Not all of them are subject to withholding tax, either. I know of one plant that paid management fees and head office administration expenses in excess of $50,000 a month, and this plant is not a huge one. These were administrative charges paid to head office. So there are also some great benefits our United States friends receive which are not all on the table.
Then we have a man like Senator Hartke from Indiana who made the statement he did on television last week. This is shocking. He must know that we have effective parity of wages with the UAW in equivalent operations in Canada and the United States, and that cars do in fact come into Canada today duty free from the United States. He also said that we are opening up doors and letting foreign imports flood us. We have a 12 per cent duty in comparison to their 3 per cent duty; this is hardly opening the door in comparison with what they are doing.

I think it is important that we make these points, because Senator Hartke is a parliamentarian as are we. From April 4 to April 8 a number of us will be in Washington with the Canada-United States parliamentary group. I believe we must make these points very clearly and watch the little distortions in regional areas such as a plant in Anderson, Indiana, or Evansville, Indiana being closed down or because a huge facility is being built in Saline, Michigan, which creates immense employment there.
There are distortions. There was the sad situation in respect of Philips of Canada which was supplying, I believe, a third of all the automotive radios for Chrysler. Then Chrysler decided to consolidate with Motorola, and Philips immediately had an immense lay-off. Parliamentarians in both the United States and Canada will be terribly sensitive about such things happening in their constituencies. Therefore, I think we must sit down and look at this matter in total. I am suggesting that we have an independent committee to look at this situation, see what the distortions are and bring them to light. Perhaps the data centre could be associated with it.
We have the International Joint Commission which deals with waterways. Maybe we could have an AJC, an automotive joint committee to help monitor these situations so that they are not distorted and so we can maintain harmony in this agreement. Such a committee cohid be comprised of labour and management as well as government representatives. I would say it should have monitoring powers. I do not think it should have executive powers. However, this would be an important element so that we would all be comparing the same things and would see our problems in proper perspective.
I believe two hon. members referred to the idea of building our own type of car in Canada. This raises a very important point about the automotive trade agreement. I have always felt that our great weakness under this agreement is the fact that we did not have the leverage of one domestically-owned automotive company. If we did, we could say to the United States that if it did not make a fair deal we would make our own automobiles and put up tariff barriers. We do not have such a company and this is not the way we operate.
We made this agreement. We said we would give it a chance. We have done so and it has worked out well. However, just because it is working well for both sides now does not mean that we want them breaking it up. We have other options, but we need leverage. One option is to build our own cars. That is a possibility. It is not beyond our technical or productive capacity. I think it would be difficult and it would take a long time. I would hope Canadians would back us up, but they do not always do that: if the car was not as good as a competitive one, they would not buy it. However, this is an option we might think about.
The other option is perhaps a joint venture with one of the foreign automotive manufacturers. This is done in other countries. Fiat and Volvo have joint ventures in other parts of the world. This might be a possibility for Canada. A model might be designed in Canada for the Canadian and American market of the type, size and style which is acceptable here and for which there is a fair market. Another option to consider is that perhaps we
March 13, 1973

could buy a position in one of the United States major companies.
When I heard last night that this debate was coming on, I did a little calculating. In our foreign exchange reserves we have $4 billion to $7 billion. I believe officially it is $4.5 billion, U.S. As I understand the balance of payments situation, we can get by with $1 billion to $li billion. Let us even say it is $2i billion-we need to keep our float orderly-and that officially we have $4.5 billion. That still leaves $2 billion. These $2 billion could be invested in the United States. The Minister of Finance could direct the Canada Development Corporation or another body to invest this money. It would still be an asset so far as the balance of payments was concerned and a loan to the CDC. We could then purchase a leverage position in a United States company.
I have just received a report from my friendly broker. Let us see what $2 billion would buy in terms of an American automobile company. General Motors has 287,604,280 shares outstanding with a price on today's market of $73 7/8 per share, for a total value of $21,245,328,163. An amount of $2 billion would buy almost 10 per cent of that. If we had a little more, we could buy 20 per cent. One could buy 25 per cent, at today's market price, for $5.34 billion.
Chrysler has 52,489,823 shares outstanding at $341 on today's market, for a total value of $1,811,243,893. We could buy the whole thing. We could go out after recessing for dinner to-night and buy it. I am not sure about the figures in respect of Chrysler because I see their assets are almost $5 billion and the shareholders' equity is $2,268 billion. However, it does seem to me that this is one type of leverage. The Ford situation is quite different because it is only worth about $7 billion. Most of that is controlled by the Ford Foundation and the Ford family. I do not think they would be willing to give up control to those of us who are here tonight.
Before sitting down I should like to say I think the following points are important. There must be co-ordination of our monitoring of this situation, as well as articulation and re-articulation of the objectives of both countries. We must reach the achievement of mutual objectives, a consultative process, a constant review of statistics including balance of payments, an arbitration function on specific short-range distortions, monitoring of the program and a report to both governments. Only in a spirit of mutual consideration for self-interest on both sides can we maintain harmony and make progress in respect of a very worth-while agreement so that both countries may benefit from it in the years ahead.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not take long. I may complete my remarks by six o'clock; at least, I shall try my best. I wondered, as did many hon. members, what would be the subject of debate to be put forth by the New Democratic Party on its allotted opposition day. They have agreed on so many points with the government and voted with them so many times that they were indeed hard pressed to find a theme for today's debate. With their well known stand on accelerated write-offs and corporate tax cuts, one would have thought they would have chosen that theme to retread the
Canada-United States Auto Pact
rip-off. After, I am sure, a very diligent search they have chosen to spend their day on the auto pack.
It is well known that the automotive agreement was whipped together in considerable haste in 1965 and was written in vague and ambiguous language. The temper of the times was different then: we had a serious trade deficit with the United States and the automotive deficit was the largest portion of our over-all trade deficit. No one can deny the auto pack has worked well and has produced an over-ali trade surplus in the automotive section of our trading account with the United States.
It is eight years or so since the agreement was signed, and we have been reappraising its effects. We have considerable difficulty in securing information on the auto pact negotiations. I think it was rather facetious of the minister to look for suggestions from this side of the House, since we are not privy to the negotiations and the points on which they are negotiating. However, on a matter as delicate as this one, I must say that I agree with the minister that it would not be wise to negotiate in public. We have, I believe, a group of highly skilled negotiators in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce who we understand keep in close touch with their U.S. counterparts.
When all the formulas are digested, the ratios and percentages calculated, we come back to two main points. The first is jobs and job security, and the second is where the philosophy of the auto pact fits into our over-all trade objectives on a long-term basis. Certainly it is understood that until we have an amicable settlement of the auto pact we cannot explore in any detail our over-all trade relations with the United States. In the balance is the future of secondary industry in Canada.
While we would like to develop secondary markets in other parts of the world for our manufactured goods, one would have to be blind to not realize that in the immediate future our trade with the United States is the keystone in our industrial development. The markets are there and we must find a way to keep the door open to Canadian products. So in our view the auto pact is vital to our future development as an industrialized nation and it is also the key to the development of secondary industry in Canada.
We are concerned about jobs and job security. Any move to lessen the number of jobs in Canada at this time would, of course, be disastrous. I am sure our negotiators would have agreed upon an acceptable package if in fact the level of unemployment in Canada had been much lower than it is. I believe it would be fair to say that the single most important factor in the auto pact discussions has been the government's preoccupation with inflation since 1968 and their acceptance of a high level of unemployment. The problem is not really an arithmetical one of ratios, percentages or even balance of trade. The real problem is that some adjustments have to be made, and while we have a high level of unemployment we cannot tolerate any change in the terms of the auto pact which would aggravate that position.
It is significant, I believe, to note at this point that the policies put forth by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact Stanfield) would in effect allow us to adjust more readily to changes in unemployment levels due to auto pact negotiations than does the cautious and ad hoc economic patchwork approach of this government. Our party's policy of running the economy at full throttle to take a large bite out of the unemployment and simultaneously impose temporary price, wage and profit controls would allow us to negotiate with much more confidence than does the economic and fiscal policy of the present government.
The hon. member for Halton (Mr. O'Connor) has detailed the minister's lack of knowledge of the auto pact, as recorded in Hansard. Hon. members will also note the numerous references to government-to-government negotiations. They will note the number of times the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) has asked about minister-to-minister negotiations. It is evident the minister is not equipped to negotiate the auto pact agreement.
There is no one on the government side with enough political clout to negotiate with people of the calibre of John Connally. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made his pilgrimage to Washington some months ago and announced a "fantastic breakthrough" in negotiations with the United States. We have not learned to this day the details of this breakthrough, but we do know that a short time later surcharges were imposed and a protectionist attitude was evident in the U.S.A. However, nowhere did we see any evidence of the fantastic breakthrough or of any special consideration for our trading position with the U.S.
There were suggestions in the Washington press recently that the U.S. position and attitude toward Canada is hardening due to the continuous critical attitude of the government toward the United States involvement in the Viet Nam war. The wisdom of the well orchestrated resolution on this grievous war during the throne speech may well haunt the trade negotiation tables for months to come.
At a time when the world is divided into rival trading blocs, the wisdom, or perhaps the lack of wisdom, on the part of the government must be questioned. At a time when we have a high level of unemployment and when the creation of new jobs and industries must be the main immediate thrust of the economic policy, we find ourselves in a serious trade negotiation with our largest customer-and we are not talking at the ministerial level. It shows how completely bankrupt this government is in the field of economic policy and planning.
We are not in a position at this time to tolerate the loss of jobs due to renegotiation of the auto pact's terms. The danger we face is twofold. The government lacks any long-term economic plan and therefore it is difficult to point to a time or period when we will be able to negotiate the auto pact so that adjustments in employment could be tolerated. We also must face up to the facts of life of secondary industry in Canada. The development of this sector of our economy must be pushed with all possible speed to aid in lowering high-level unemployment in Canada. While the trade irritants remain between our two nations, we will be hard pressed to find the additional markets we will require.

It is evident that we are facing very serious negotiations in the months ahead. I believe that our negotiators are knowledgeable persons who are capable of handling these matters, and are dedicated to their task of protecting Canada's position. It is unfortunate that our negotiators cannot bargain from the strength of an economic policy that is expansionist and designed to cope with the economic problems that face us. With such policies, they could feel reasonably assured that we could adjust to any disruption caused by changes in the terms of the auto pact and take up any unemployment slack elsewhere in our economy. In the long run, the big losers are our secondary industries, not only those presently operating who would expand but the new ones we so desperately need to employ our ever expanding labour force.
There is no doubt that we face hard times ahead in our trade negotiations with the United States. I am not concerned about the negotiations themselves; I am concerned about those at the cabinet level charged with responsibility to direct and carry out this delicate task. In my view, they are leading from weakness as a government lacking in sound economic programs, as they have so amply demonstrated over the past four years.
Let me say in closing that I can only wish the negotiators well. The government has indeed failed to develop a policy that would benefit Canadians and resolve the conflict concerning the Canada-U.S. automotive agreement, as stated in the motion of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). This makes the task of the negotiators extremely difficult. If the government is not capable of preparing economic programs that will allow us to negotiate from strength, then they should move over and let those on this side of the House, who have a clear picture of what is required, get on with the job.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a representative of an automotive community I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate on the Canada-U.S. auto pact. Windsor accounts for approximately 25 per cent of the total Canadian output of automotive products and has benefited more than any other Canadian centre from the auto pact. Production of motor vehicles increased in Windsor by 112 per cent from 1964 to 1971, as opposed to 105 per cent for the whole country, and in the same period employment in the "Big Three" in Windsor jumped by 41 per cent, as opposed to 33 per cent for the whole country including Windsor.
Since Windsor has much to lose from any unfavourable change in the auto pact, my colleagues the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Consumer and
March 13, 1973

Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray) and I have been vigilant in our concern about the future of the pact. Were it not for their cabinet responsibilities I know that they, too, would be speaking in this debate.
Like every other bargain, the pact has its advantages and its disadvantages. To assess its value on an over-all basis we need some kind of balance sheet. Let us first look at it from the viewpoint of employment, Mr. Speaker. Employment in Canada in the automotive industry rose from 68,400 in November, 1964, through 81,400 in November, 1970, to 91,600 in November 1971, to 97,100 in November, 1972. This is an increase of 28,700, or close to 30,000 in the eight-year span from 1964 to 1972.
As the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) mentioned this afternoon, there is a multiplier effect for these figures. Whether you take the multiplier as one, two or three, as he pointed out the number of additional jobs created in our country by this great advance under the auto pact is considerable indeed. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, employment under the pact, is about equally divided between those involved in the production of parts and accessories, on the one hand, and those involved in assembly on the other hand.
Looking at the same balance sheet from the point of view of trade, we find that in 1964 Canada had a deficit of $602 million with the United States. In 1971 there was a $197 million surplus in our favour; and in 1972, if this is the final figure, it was $5.8 million in our favour. So, Mr. Speaker, we can see that our annual trade under the auto pact with the United States is now roughly in balance. But this of course means that there has been a spectacular gain on Canada's part. We are about $1 billion ahead in vehicle assembly and about $1 billion behind in parts, so that together we come out roughly even across the whole spectrum.
Another way of looking at our progress under the auto pact is this. It used to be said that Canadians bought about 7.5 per cent of the total North American auto market but produced only about 4 per cent. Actually, these figures were totally misleading because the former included profits and the latter did not. For this reason these figures are not used any more. The accurate way of looking at it is by considering our trade balance. We now produce approximately what we consume in the auto market.
Looking at the situation from the point of view of the so-called safeguards, we are spectacularly ahead of where we were in 1964. With regard to the first safeguard concerning vehicle production, the ratio of vehicles produced in Canada to vehicles sold in Canada was in the area of 90 per cent to 100 per cent in 1964, and in 1972 it had climbed to the area of 130 per cent to 140 per cent. With respect to the Canadian value added safeguard, we are about $1 billion ahead of where we were in 1964.
Turning, in our balance sheet, to the question of prices we find a more marginal advantage. As the minister pointed out this afternoon, there has been progress in narrowing the price differential; it has decreased by about one half since 1964. This means that Canadian automotive prices have risen only about half as fast as those in the United States.
Canada-United States Auto Pact
There are also certain disadvantages as there would be in any agreement. Among the disadvantages under the auto pact are the control of purchasing in the United States, except for General Motors in Oshawa, and the fact that there is very little design or engineering done in Canada. So that we have a gain in the assembly of automobiles rather than in parts, and we have gained many unskilled jobs but have lost some skilled employment.
In summary, I should like to see the marginal advance with respect to prices increased, and the disadvantages reversed, in any renegotiation, but in my view and that of my colleagues, we have on balance gained very substantially under the pact. The question with regard to the renegotiation of the pact is that of where our priorities are. Canada's original objectives with respect to the auto pact were an increase in production, efficiency and employment in the Canadian automotive industry and a better break for the Canadian consumer. My first priority is Canadian jobs, protection of our gains and the continuance of our advance with respect to jobs for Canadians in the automotive industry. I would put in a lower place the reducing of prices for Canadian consumers. Here I detect a certain waffling, if I may use that word, in the resolution as phrased. If I may draw the attention of the House to this, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent) moved:
That this House deplores the failure of the government to develop beyond the 1965 Canada-United States automotive agreement a policy which would benefit Canadians and which would contribute to resolving Canada-United States conflict in this area to the mutual benefit of both countries; and this House, therefore, urges the government to take certain immediate steps to lower the prices of automobiles to Canadian consumers and to protect the jobs of Canadian autoworkers.
This resolution apparently accords equal priority to lowering prices and to protecting the jobs of Canadians. I do not think that this is a tenable position, Mr. Speaker, and I think it is crucial that we have our priorities straight before we talk, as did the hon. member for Oshawa-Whit-by and his colleagues, about renegotiating the pact with the United States.
The problem with the position of the NDP is even more fundamental when we consider the proposals which the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) made this afternoon. The auto pact is a free trade pact on the United States side, but it is not on the Canadian side. On our side it is, rather, a duty-remission plan. I should like to direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the words of the pact itself. Article I reads:
The governments of Canada and the United States, pursuant to the above principles, shall seek the early achievement of the following objectives:
(a)	The creation of a broader market for automotive products within which the full benefits of specialization and large-scale production can be achieved:
(b)	The liberalization of Canadian and United States automotive trade in respect of tariff barriers and other factors tending to impede it, with a view to enabling the industries of both countries to participate on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total market of the two countries;
2184

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact
(c)	The development of conditions in which market forces may
operate effectively to attain the most economic pattern of investment, production and trade.
I believe that the most relevant of these objectives for the present discussion is (b) which is stated to be, most particularly:
The liberalization of Canadian and United States automotive trade in respect of tariff barriers-
But we have to advert immediately to the qualification which follows the initial statement of the principle, which would otherwise suggest a free trade position. But the clause goes on to point out:
-with a view to enabling the industries of both countries to participate on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total market of the two countries;
It is my contention, Mr. Speaker, that a fair and equitable basis for Canadian participation and for the participation of Canadian industry in the automotive market does not mean free trade. It may always be necessary- not just for a transitional period-if there is to be participation by Canadian industries on a fair and equitable basis, there should be limitation on the free trade principle on our side. In taking such a position, we should not be contravening the auto pact; we should rather be following it because we should be conforming to the objective of liberalization of trade on the conditions imposed by the agreement itself.
There are under the pact two so-called safeguards, but one of the other protections which exists on our side is a tariff according to which recognized Canadian manufacturers are allowed to import duty free into Canada provided certain conditions are observed. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby agrees that we should not attempt to reach complete free trade with the United States, but he proposes the abandonment of the duty-remission plan. On the one hand, he says let us retain the production safeguard and the Canadian added value safeguard although both are admittedly inoperative because our industry has done extremely well under the pact. On the other hand, he argues that we should abandon the one protection that is operative. But, if we remove the duty, we remove the duty-remission feature with it. We cannot very well retain the duty protection for ensuring Canadian objectives if there is no duty there.
I realize that in order to lower car prices in Canada the hon. member has proposed removing the 15 per cent Canadian duty only for individuals who wish to purchase cars in the United States and not necessarily, he might argue, for automotive companies. That would be as impossible in practice as it is simple in theory. Companies can hardly be denied what is legitimate for individuals- importing cars from the United States without duty and without limitation. If they were, they could retaliate by refraining from further investment in Canada. Worse still, we would be playing into the hands of the American government, whose principal policy objective this removal of duty has been.
This was quite plainly stated by Mr. Philip Tresize when he was in Canada in October. This gentleman was, until he resigned, one of the leading American officials of the United States concerned with the auto pact. Speaking on the pact in Toronto, he publicly advocated not only scrap-

ping the two so-called safeguards, but also the removal of the tariff arrangement that is presently in effect.

The sell-out is what I am talking about. It is what you are proposing. Although the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby did not say so clearly, what he probably had in mind was not unilateral Canadian action to cut out the tariff, but a new auto pact in which we would give up the tariff in return for new safeguards at the 1972 level of production rather than at the 1964 level. If this is his proposal it is a major policy proposal on behalf of the NDP calling for renegotiation of the auto pact. Such a proposal obviously needs to be thoroughly worked through by experts before a definitive answer can be given.
However, my initial reaction to it is twofold. First, if it were to have any further advantage for Canada it is unrealistic to think that the United States would agree. The United States' desire to renegotiate the pact now is based on the feeling that it is already too favourable to Canada. It has been described by one United States senator as foreign aid to Canada. Secondly, it would seem to me to have a short-term advantage for Canada, but longterm disadvantages. In the short run, the 1972 base would obviously be advantageous, given a slight recession in the immediately following years. In a few years, however, it would become inoperative, just as the 1964 figures have become inoperative, by reason of the progress of our industry. Then we would have nothing left to bargain with in future because we would have given up our main bargaining tool, the tariff, in 1973.
My feeling that the NDP proposal is working in the direction of free trade is strengthened by the remarks the hon. member for Fraser Valley West made subsequent to those of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby in which I believe he was supporting free trade in the used car market. I would not want to be unduly harsh on the proposal of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. I appreciate the thought he has given to it and the fact that he has put it forward in good faith, but I wish he had put it forward more unambiguously and had faced the consequences more squarely. Still it is a proposal to which serious thought must be given by the government. However, I believe it is to some extent the product of a mentality which is trying at the same time to please everybody, in this case both workers and consumers, with more jobs and lower prices. In such an equation I know on which side I belong. I stand with the automotive workers and their jobs. I will continue to press the government for policies which will maintain and increase employment in the automotive industry in Canada. I hope other hon. members will be equally forthright in facing the choices that have to be made on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, it may seem strange that a member representing Niagara Falls should speak in this debate. However, although the peninsula is noted more for its tourism and agriculture than for its involvement in this particular industry, the workers in the auto industry form a large part of our total labour
March 13, 1973

force. In Thorold there is the Hayes-Dana plant, in Niagara Falls there is the Ford Glass plant, and in St. Catharines there are GM subsidiaries known as MacKinnon's and Thompson Products.
Without doubt, all these industries have benefited from this pact. More recently, however, 120 jobs have been lost to the area following the transfer of production of the Maverick brake-drum to the United States. The labour force at MacKinnon's has been reduced to around the 6,400 mark, having been at 7,200 in 1966. I was speaking today to the head of the union at MacKinnon's, who is greatly concerned about these movements in production. What has happened will affect the rest of the workers who live in the peninsula, particularly those who use Niagara Falls, my riding, as a dormitory area.
One year ago last December, when Mr. Pepin went south and when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) also went south at about the time my party's annual meeting was being held in Ottawa, we heard that all was well with the auto pact. It now appears that all was not well. Despite what the minister has said, I suggest we have reached the point of stalemate. A new beginning must be made. New initiatives must be undertaken because, as the last speaker suggested, Senator Hartke has been saying that the automotive agreement was granted as a boon from the American government. He said that the pact is foreign aid.
Although I do not read as many newspapers as I should like to read, I have not heard statements advanced on this question by the minister. I suggest that we must review the whole situation and come to some commonly accepted agreement as to figures that ought to be used. The American government uses one set of figures and we use another. We must redefine what each is to obtain from this automotive pact now and in the future.
I submit that this pact ought to bring about stability in the area of automotive production. That is important. In addition, not only the governments are involved in this area. We must be certain for whom governments speak. If they speak for the companies, I submit they should also speak on behalf of the workers and for the consumers in our communities. It is in the interest of the governments on both sides of the border to argue on behalf of their respective citizens.
Certainly, in my estimation, the companies are placed in a most difficult position. The reason is that the automobile manufacturers are international companies and subject to pressures from both governments. The automobile manufacturing companies are probably more affected by pressure from the U.S. government than by pressure from the Canadian government. Therefore, one is led to wonder whether the drop in Canada's trade position has been the result of the play of "free market forces" or the result of company reaction to United States government pressures of both the stick and carrot variety, that is, of pressures to move successful production lines southward, as happened for example in the case of the Ste. Therese plant in which production of the successful Pontiac model was shipped south. The less successful Vega model was produced in place of that model, the result being that the work force of some 2,300 has been reduced to 1,100. One can imagine the impact of that reduction on the community. Or one can
Canada-United States Auto Pact
mention pressures being exerted under the DISC program which makes it more profitable for a company to produce cars in the United States than in Canada.
The companies are in a difficult position. It may well be that to guarantee long-range Canadian growth the Canadian government, in view of the experience we have obtained with this industry, must for the sake of the workers and consumers of this country give the companies what may be termed a positive arguing point; that is, those companies must be able to say to the United States government that they have entered into contractual relationships with the Canadian government which they must honour. They must be able to say this to the American government.
Certainly experience in free trade, especially in the farm machinery industry, has clearly shown that new production facilities do not develop in Canada but develop in the United States. This experience certainly goes back to 1949. For that reason it is my opinion that in no circumstances can we accept a completely uncontrolled situation. There must be guarantees somewhere along the line. Equality of production must be guaranteed for our workers and consumers. The Canadian subsidiaries of American automotive companies cannot be placed in the position of having to stand alone against United States government pressure.
The affected workers, their families and the communities in which they live and of which they form the economic base are very much affected by the pact. Although the automative workers, as workers in any industry, must accept the vagaries of the market it is unreasonable to expect them to be subjected to pressures which can quickly disrupt the life of an entire community. Once again I refer to the example of Ste. Therese. There a whole community was built around a certain automotive producing facility. There, after a certain number of jobs had been built up, the labour force was suddenly reduced. This could also happen in Talbotville or our own area.
Stability in the industry must be achieved so far as possible. Only new initiatives, only a review from the bottom up can achieve this. Canadian workers recognize, I believe, that although solidarity with their American brothers may be a desirable theme, certain of their American brothers put their own jobs first and cannot be relied on to protect Canadian workers' interests.

government can protect our workers, in conjunction with the workers themselves. It is on our government that our workers must rely. The auto pact has been instrumental in the building of new communities and has increased the prosperity of older ones. The interests of those communities must be protected. For that reason stability must be introduced.
Before leaving the subject of workers may I say that it is my understanding, on the basis of many sources of information, that the Canadian worker has certainly done his share in making this pact successful. In MacKinnon's plant in St. Catharines, and in other plants, the quality of
2186

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact production has been higher than in corresponding parent plants in the United States. There has been less loss of time for various causes. There has been less pilfering and less absenteeism due to alcohol or drug use. So our Canadian workers are every bit as good as American workers, if not better. Actually, our productivity has reached the point at which possible disparities due to our northern clime can be ignored. Market forces, along with increased productivity, have made our production facilities in Canada the equal of United States facilities.
If Canadian production is competitive with that in the United States the consumer may well ask, why are automobiles, both cars and trucks, more expensive in Canada and why has the differential in price, which had been dropping, risen recently? There must be three reasons for this differential: natural forces such as weather and the smaller number of units being serviced, government tax structures or company pricing policies. To my mind those are the only possibilities we ought to consider. I suggest that they must be clearly identified in the public mind so that people may either accept the need for the differential, if it is the result of natural forces, or bring pressure to bear on their government if it is not.
Canadians have always paid a price for being Canadian. We have accepted this in all generations to this point and I believe we will now. But that price must be fairly put before Canadians and these costs must be legitimate. The governments of the two countries must recognize that this auto pact has been of benefit to both countries. It has been somewhat less so than anticipated because of the high rate of imported cars being sold in Canada. Here, again, a clear and comprehensive study starting from square one must be undertaken to clearly point out how this hurts us, if it does, and what alternative actions exist.
In summation, it is in the interests of all concerned, governments, producers, workers, communities and consumers, to have a clear picture of what has been a mutually beneficial relationship. It is in the interests of all to redefine the aims and arrive at stable patterns in so far as this can be done.
That a thorough review is necessary can be proven, not only by the lack of any movement for a long period but by the inane ravings of Senator Hartke that this pact came about as a form of foreign aid, when in fact it came about as the result of pressures to build Canadian industry, initiated by the Conservative government in the early sixties-
