When we were discussing the auto pact in 1966, a number of reasons were put forward by the government for proposing this pact. It was said that if we entered into this agreement with the United States it would increase employment. That, of course, has happened. We were told that it would cut down on the deficit in the trade balance between Canada and the United States. While that has happened, the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville was very careful how he quoted those figures. He skated over the record of the past year. The trade surplus in our favour which was apparent in the early seventies virtually disappeared last year. Instead of a trade surplus this year and next, we will probably again have a trade deficit with the United States.
There is a third important point which the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville does not understand. Until the hon. member and the government understand this point the Liberal party will not win seats outside the golden triangle in Ontario. We were told that the auto pact would result in a price reduction for Canadian consumers. I wish to quote from two editorials which appeared in 1965 in newspapers which support the Liberal government. They were discussing the auto pact. I do this to show the minister and the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville what the people outside of Windsor expect from the auto pact. I quote from the Vancouver Sun, which as far as I know has always supported the Liberal party, of April 14, 1965:
Among other things, Mr. Walter Gordon's forthcoming budget will have to defend the Canadian-American free trade deal in automotive products.
It can be easily defended if it means that automobile prices will soon fall. If they don't, the deal is quite indefensible.
The Winnipeg Free Press, a newspaper in my city-and there is no more partisan supporter of Liberal government in Canada-when discussing the auto pact wrote on April 17, 1965:
A much larger question now faces the Canadian government as a result of the free trade deal. It is whether this ostensibly constructive agreement will do any good for the Canadian consumer
March 13, 1973

or whether it will benefit only a few rich automobile manufacturers.
The Free Press asked the question. The answer is now very clear. We are in fact subsidizing and benefiting the large automobile manufacturers.

To my knowledge, there is no department of government in Ottawa which has more high-priced, supposed expert civil servants than the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. To try to find out from that department whether it has made any studies with regard to the relative cost of producing cars in Canada compared to the cost of producing cars in the United States, or the relative profits of Canadian automobile companies compared to the profits of their United States parent corporations, is an impossibility. The minister will not tell Members of Parliament and the public whether such studies have been made. They certainly ought to have been made. If they have, their results are being hidden. If not, the minister and the government should be condemned, because that would be a dereliction of duty. If studies have been made, the results must be so bad that the government is afraid to let the Canadian people know the facts.
Fortunately, there are people in Canada who are not civil servants. There are some journalists. I suggest to the minister that in all likelihood their salaries are substantially less than the salaries of the officials in his department who should be making this kind of study.
I do not have time to put on record all the facts in the articles written by Mr. Thomas Claridge and Mr. John Rolfe in March and April of 1972, but let me summarize as briefly as I can some of the statements contained in these articles. I quote, for example, from the article of April 20, 1972, by Mr. Claridge:
The typical Canadian new car buyer is paying an extra $300 for a North American built automobile because of a manufacturers' pricing policy now under investigation by the federal government.
Under the policies being followed by all four Canadian car manufacturers, Canadian car dealers are being charged about 10 per cent more than U.S. dealers for cars built in Canada.
They made an investigation, and they sure as hell gave the results. The old excuses, the old rationalization given for higher prices in Canada disappears. The old rationalization was that the production runs in Canada were so much shorter that we could not turn out cars here as cheaply as in the United States.
As I have said, I do not have time to put forward all the facts that Mr. Claridge and Mr. Rolfe have embodied in these articles; but we find that cars built in Canadian plants in Ontario, cars built in St. Thomas, are being exported to the United States and sold for $250 to $300 less in Buffalo than in Toronto.

Canada-United States Auto Pact
American Motors car in Buffalo or in upstate New York for $300 less than they can in Hamilton or Toronto, and they are not losing money, there is only one conclusion you can draw. This is the conclusion the writers in the Globe and Mail have come to. It is that Canadian consumers are being overcharged between $250 and $300 per car.
The writers I have named analysed the profit per unit made by automobile companies in Canada compared with the profit per unit made by the same companies in the United States. What did they find? They found that for the last year for which figures are available the per unit profit in Canada was between $225 to $250 more than it was in the United States.
Who was making that possible? The Canadian consumer. He was paying in two ways. He was paying up to $300 more for the car, and he was also paying in another way. Before the auto pact was concluded, the Canadian government was getting, in the form of excise duties on cars and car parts imported into Canada from the United States, in the neighbourhood of $50 million. The Canadian taxpayer does not get the benefit of that $50 million any more. Thanks to the generosity of the Liberal government, it goes to increase the profits of General Motors, Chrysler, Ford and American Motors. This is the government which represent the ordinary taxpayers of this country.
The record as to what has happened is clear. We have not just criticized the government because the Canadian consumer is paying more; we have outlined a method by which the Canadian consumer would benefit from lower car prices. What my hon. friend from Oshawa-Whitby has proposed is that we give to the individual Canadian consumer the same right as we have given to the "Big Three" automobile companies. We permit them to manufacture cars in the United States and bring them into Canada without paying excise duty of 15 per cent.
The fact is that the Canadian subsidiaries of these multinational automobile corporations have been overcharging Canadian consumers. They have been making exorbitant profits. We are saying that if the Canadian consumer can go to the United States and purchase a car without paying the duty, the Canadian subsidiaries of the big automobile companies should be obliged to reduce the price they charge the Canadian consumer by the amount they overcharge, which is demonstrated to be between $250 and $300 per car.
The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville has trotted out the bogey that if you do that, United States manufacturers will simply cut out production in Canada. I suggest that no corporation, having invested billions of dollars in plant and equipment in this country, will stop production. They want a return on their investment and they are entitled to a legitimate return. We are objecting to the exorbitant profits they are making.
There is, I realize, a problem. We have the nonsense of Senator Hartke to deal with, and the protectionist sentiment which is growing in the United States. So what my hon. friend suggests is that we protect the Canadian auto industry by renegotiating the automobile agreement in such a way that Canadian production and the Canadian value added requirement would be dependent, not upon production in Canada, not upon the consumption of cars

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact
built in Canada but on the consumption by Canadians of cars purchased anywhere in North America. If this were done and the minimum production floor were based on 1972 rather than 1965 levels, we could reduce the price of cars to Canadian consumers and protect the jobs of Canadian workers.
I do not believe the United States government would object too strenuously to this kind of negotiation, because it is not that government which would be hurt; it is, rather, the Canadian subsidiaries of the United States corporations-and I do not think that even President Nixon worries too much about them.
There is one more thing which this proposal would do. According to statistics given us by the minister's department, somewhere between 20 and 25 per cent of all new cars purchased in Canada are imported from countries such as Japan, Sweden, Germany and Italy. That is almost twice as high as the percentage of new cars this country imports from the United States. I suggest the reason for this disparity is the exorbitant and excessive price charged the Canadian consumer for these new cars. I suggest that if we forced these companies to cut back on the price, Canadian consumers would in increasing numbers buy Canadian-built cars. I suggest this would be good for the companies, good for the consumers and good for Canadian automotive workers.
The hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville said one correct thing when he suggested that this proposal was worthy of study. I suggest to the minister that he give it a great deal more study than the non-studies we have had from him up to now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a lot of speeches today about the auto pact agreement which goes back to 1965. We have heard those who spoke for it, those who spoke against it and those who are waffling in between. If we listened intently to speakers on the government side we would be under the impression that this was the greatest thing that ever happened to Canada. The important thing is that this is one of the most vital manufacturing industries in this country, which produces a tremendous number of jobs. If the safeguards are taken out of the agreement as far as production levels are concerned, this industry will suffer terribly and we will be forced to go back and hammer at the minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission.
March 13, 1973

Because we have heard a lot of speeches this afternoon and this evening, I do not intend to prolong this debate. I will not speak at length on this motion as many hon. members from all parties have done so already. I do wish to speak about one or two related issues which I feel are of prime importance to Canada as a whole and to consumers and auto workers in particular.
It seems to me that in general economic and industrial matters we in Canada are always taking a back seat to our United States neighbours, and perhaps I should say our United States entrepreneurs to the south. Whenever there is a crisis in trade or monetary matters, it is we who go cap in hand to Washington to come to some agreement in these areas. I certainly hope the Minister of Inudstry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) will not bow to United States pressure over the automotive agreement signed in 1965. If he does, Canadian consumers of automobiles, and auto workers in Canada will suffer. As I said earlier, if this does happen many more workers will be added to the unemployment insurance rolls.
It appears to me that if the so-called safeguards in the auto pact are abolished, Canadians will continue to pay from $200 to $300 more for a car purchased in Canada than our United States friends pay for the same type of car when it crosses the border and is sold in the United States. I find this situation deplorable. I do not know why this government in the past eight years could not have renegotiated the agreement and avoided that kind of travesty.
When one considers that an academic study carried out last year revealed that the four major automotive companies, Ford Motor Company, Chrysler, General Motors and American Motors charged their dealers in Canada about $250 more for a standard, identical car produced in Canada than is charged in the United States, one wonders what advantages accrue to the Canadian consumer or the Canadian car buyer even with the present safeguards. This is totally unfair and I suggest many people in Canada are becoming completely fed up with the unfair situation. I should like to ask a simple question: Why does the federal government allow this travesty to exist when involved are the same parts, the same materials and the same or even slightly lower wages in Canada? Even with this situation, we in Canada pay substantially more under this supposedly free trade agreement. I mentioned a short while ago the $100 tax credit. If a person purchases a small American car made in this country, the extra money he would pay would wipe out that $100 tax credit which is mentioned in the budget.
If I might refer to the remarks made earlier today made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), he said there is no economic justification for this pricing policy. In point of fact it is sheer corporate profiteering at the expense of the Canadian public. Several years ago a one-man royal commission on the automotive industry said that it would be disastrous for Canada not to have safeguards in the automotive trade agreement with the United States. When we deal with such large job-creating industries as General Motors, Ford, Chrysler and American Motors which are almost 100 per cent American owned, there would be no guarantee that Canada would
Canada-United States Auto Pact
get her share of future growth in the automotive industry or that current production levels would be maintained; hence the production safeguard principle in the pact.
When looking at the excessive profits reaped by just one of these oligopoly-controlled industries, Ford, one finds that the unit profit of that industry in Canada was $222 higher than the per unit profit of the American parent. The other companies would be similar, in my opinion. The per unit profit for Ford of Canada increased in each of the four most recent years for which figures are available: in 1968 it was $117; in 1969 it was $164; in 1970 it was $153; in 1971 it was $228. The figures are obviously approximately the same for Chrysler and General Motors.
On the other hand, the duty remissions which the companies got from the Canadian taxpayer as a result of the pact were as follows: Ford, $176,614,083; American Motors, $3,135,075; Chrysler, $1,992,602; General Motors, $1,388,150. I am wondering whether any of these corporations are on the list of 95 corporations from which the Liberal Party receives its political slush funds, and the Tories too; let us not forget them.
Let us look at the situation in Talbotville where Ford of Canada has been manufacturing for some years a small compact car, I believe called the Pinto. The men who produce this automobile in Canada have to pay $200 to $300 more than the same car manufactured in Canada sells for in Detroit; and that car has to be transported some 125 miles from the production plant in Talbotville to the car lot in Detroit. Is this economic justice? The Liberals have allowed this situation to exist year after year. I have yet to find a reasonable explanation for this anomaly and for this travesty.
The budget gave taxpayers a $100 tax credit and all the people of Canada thought it was great. We thought it was good, too, considering the fact that we had finally convinced the Liberal government that tax credits were far superior to regressive basic tax reductions. But those who purchase a Pinto in Canada lose that tax credit and more because of the present ridiculous pricing of Canadian-built cars vis-a-vis the United States.
This may be the right time to begin producing an allCanadian car, not just for nationalistic reasons-indeed, I hope not-but a family car designed and engineered in Canada and built by Canadian workers. When I refer to workers I am not referring merely to those who work on the assembly line; I am referring also to the designers of cars, the engineers and the technical people involved. Must we continue to be the child of our great United States "big daddy"? If Sweden, approximately one-third the size of Canada, can do it and become world renowned for so doing-not only for building cars but for building engines, including marine engines-what is the matter with us?

I would also like to comment on the extra cost that Canadians face when buying an automobile in the west. Why should westerners pay more-simply because they are Canadians living farther away from the automobile manufacturers in central Canada? Cannot we adjust freight rates to accommodate our fellow citizens who happen to live in the west or in the Maritimes? What is wrong with the proposal to set up different freight rates?
Another concern of mine relates to the farm implement industry. This concern is very close to me because my home town of Brantford is a major manufacturer of farm implements. If the safeguards in the auto pact go down the drain, will the U.S.-Canada agreement on the manufacturing of farm implements follow? May I say in conclusion that I feel that at present we are ready to sell out to the United States certain safeguards in the auto pact, which will eventually have a detrimental effect both on our consumers and our auto workers. I sincerely hope that the government will keep Canada in mind as the negotiations continue. It seems to me that in all fields of manufacturing, particularly so far as natural resources are concerned, we are constantly selling out to the much more powerful nation to the south. A good time to stop this is right now when the auto pact safeguards are up for grabs-for American grabs!
Let us not become angry and irritated, or in fact irrational. Let us all begin to think in terms of economic and monetary justice in an objective, mature and realistic manner. We do not hate the Americans, but we will be damned if we will continue to live every day under this threat of American domination when I am convinced that we have the manpower, the ingenuity and the will in this country, and indeed we have the capital, to go ahead and

make something for ourselves in this world, not in a chauvinistic way but in a creative and competitive way. This is what we need, and we have not been getting it from this government for the past ten years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be taking part in this debate on the supply motion introduced by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whit-by (Mr. Broadbent) and his party. However, I am at a loss to understand, in the knowledge that we could vote for such a motion, why the hon. member did not introduce it as a non-confidence motion. Let him not say that he could not do it because of the rules, because the rules do not prohibit his party from introducing a non-confidence motion if they wish. Their House leader had only to make arrangements with the other House leaders that they be granted one confidence vote; they would have had to give 24 hours written notice, after which they could have presented a non-confidence motion here today. However, they did not see fit to do that. They continue to talk and condemn the government but they do not speak in accordance with the way in which they vote.
However, we have had a good discussion here tonight on the Canada-U.S. auto pact. I think it is one of the best opportunities we have had to discuss this important subject matter. Everybody seems to be pretty well in accord regarding the Canada-U.S. auto pact, not necessarily so far as all its features are concerned, but in agreement with most of them. But if it is so good, may I remind the House that it was the late Mr. Nowlan, then minister of national revenue, who realized the seriousness of the situation in the car industry in Canada and the great imbalance of trade which we had at that time. Therefore he appointed a one-man commission composed of Professor Blake. Those were the days when we did not hear about white papers, task forces and all those things which we hear about so much today.
Professor Blake of the University of Toronto conceived a very interesting idea which he presented to the manufacturers of auto parts in Canada, that the duty on every car engine that was imported to Canada, assembled and then exported be remitted. This plan proved to be very successful. Then the Liberal party came to power and we had what we called the "Drury Mach I" version of the auto pact. This Mach I version was simply an extension of the Blake formula. It was very successful until one of the companies manufacturing radiators in the United States objected and took their case to the U.S. Supreme Court. Rather than lose the case, Canada withdrew and sat down to negotiate the Canada-U.S. auto pact. That is, in brief, the history of this pact.
When I say we have had a good discussion of this matter today, I must point out that we certainly did not have an opportunity to discuss the subject when the Canada-U.S. auto pact was first introduced by order in council. The late Mr. Pearson and some officials of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce flew to President Johnson's ranch, and after being wined and dined they signed the treaty. I suppose they were first told that it was a good thing for the "Big Three" car manufacturers. So the treaty was signed and brought back to Canada but we, the elected representatives of the Canadian people, never had an opportunity to debate the treaty.
March 13, 1973

It is interesting to refej~ to history once in a while when you speak of such things as treaties. I was interested to learn that Mr. Mackenzie King, in June of 1926, had the following to say:
-before His Majesty's Canadian ministers advise ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signify acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
My, how things have changed since the present government has taken over! On April 12, 1928, in the course of a debate on the international sanitary convention, the same right hon. gentleman said this:
I submit that the day has passed when any government or executive should feel that they should take it upon themselves without the approval of parliament, to commit a country to obligations involving any considerable financial outlays or active undertakings. In all cases where obligations of such a character are being assumed internationally, parliament itself should be assured of having the full right of approving what is done before binding commitments are made. I would not confine parliamentary approval only to those matters which involve military sanctions and the like. I feel parliamentary approval should apply where there are involved matters of large expenditure or political considerations of a far-reaching character.
Those were the words the late Mackenzie King used. I hope you will pardon me if I wander a little off this subject, Mr. Speaker, but recently the government decided that a peace corps should go to Viet Nam. That was a treaty or arrangement-I don't know which-that was never discussed in this House. But after our troops were sent over there the government invited us to go along and see how things were making out. I repeat that we never had a chance to discuss it. My, how things have changed! Is that how the Canada-U.S. auto pact was brought about?
The auto pact has had a stormy passage. It has had its ups and downs, its arounds and abouts. It has had its good points and its bad points. It has been called a free trade treaty. I ask, free trade for whom? It is free trade for the car manufacturers, but not for Canadian citizens who subsidize the program. They are not getting the benefit of the free trade operations. It is certainly free trade when an American can come over to Canada, buy a car here and take it back duty free. But no American would be foolish enough to do that because he would have to pay more for his car here than he would pay in the United States. But if Canadians go to the United States and buy cars there, they have to pay 15 per cent duty when they bring those cars back to Canada.
The auto treaty will never be successful until there is at least parity of price between what the Canadian has to pay for a car manufactured in Canada and what the American has to pay for the same type of car when he buys it in Detroit. Why should we have to pay $300 or $400 more for a car made here in our own backyard when, after transporting it 300 miles across the border, Americans can buy it there for $300 less?
When this car treaty was introduced, Canadians agreed to cut tariffs by $50 million a year. Each and every year the car treaty has been in effect we have forgone that $50 million in tariffs. On top of that we give the car manufac-
Canada-United States Auto Pact
turers a considerable remission in duties. I am not going to belabour the House with all the details, but $80 million was given to one car manufacturer. This was brought to the attention of the House by the Auditor General. When the public accounts committee looked into the matter it uncovered a lot of interesting information, part of which has not been reported back to the House even to this day. The Auditor General said on that occasion that he does not audit the books of Canada except according to the legislation laid down by parliament. He does not audit those books according to notes, memoranda or letters written by people in high places.
This was the method by which the car manufacturers obtained their remission of duty. A letter was written by one of the companies and it was responded to by the then minister of industry. The government should have amended the treaty in such a way that the Auditor General could look on the transaction as straightforward, but there was an oversight on the part of the government. The pact was not amended and those remissions of millions of dollars were still given to the car manufacturers.
Along with that little bonanza, plus the $50 million tariff cut, there is now the DISC program. On March 17, 1972, the then minister of industry, trade and commerce was asked if the American car manufacturers were using the DISC program and he advised this House that they were not. But a week later he advised the House that he had misinformed it and that the American car manufacturers were using the DISC program. No apology was forthcoming from either the car manufacturers or the minister. The DISC program gives American car manufacturers a tremendous advantage. I maintain that they have no right to use it when they still operate under the Canada-U.S. car pact. Now they are getting things both ways, using DISC and the auto pact. To the best of my knowledge, they are still using DISC. I would like the minister to correct me if that is not the case.
But despite the advantages and the subsidies which the car manufacturers are getting, Canadians still have to pay more for a car made in Canada than Americans pay for the same car in their country. You cannot blame the Canadian people for being annoyed at this. People talk about the great advantages of the car pact. I realize that we have corrected our imbalance in trade, in dollars and cents, but when we ask whether we have improved our trade balance so far as manpower is concerned, a big question mark remains.
Everybody realizes that the major components of cars, such as differentials, transmissions and carburetors- those parts which require a lot of man-hours to manufacture-are made in the United States, brought into Canada duty free and here assembled in cars. We are nothing more than a bunch of "puter-oners" of nuts and bolts. This is a disgraceful situation. We are entitled to a higher ranking in the technological field than that of "puter-oner" of nuts and bolts. We should be making these parts in Canada.
The latest figures I have show that from January to June, 1971, we imported $1,208,540,000 worth of automotive parts from the United States and we exported automotive part to the United States worth only $660,385,000. In other words, we import about 200 times more value

March 13, 1973
Canada-United States Auto Pact in parts than we export. That proves beyond a shadow of doubt that we are importing the major components of cars and that we are purely and simply assembly-line operators. I am sure this situation can be remedied.
I see that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker. There are other matters I should have liked to have gone into, but I will simply say that I hope the minister will not weaken one bit on the stand he takes with his American counterparts when negotiating this treaty. Goodness knows, it is two years overdue now: it was a five-year pact, due to be renegotiated in 1970. The minister must be firm in these deliberations; he must not give an inch on the safety factors involved nor the Canadian content. I know we are well over the market now, but the time will come when we will not have the great surplus we have had in the past, and those safety features must be retained. When it comes to trade, I hope the minister remembers that we are the proud possessors of a great wealth of natural resources and that he has one of the best bargaining clubs held by any Canadian minister.

Mr. Speaker, the government welcomes the motion before the House, for it gives us the opportunity to talk about the auto pact and to tell the House and the general public how this agreement, which was proposed by a Liberal government, has been to the advantage of Canadians and how we expect it to continue being so.
Although the motion itself is somewhat lacking in coherence, the subject is definitely welcome.
The hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Caouette) spoke this afternoon about the problem of the snowmobile industry. It is clear that the industry is experiencing growing pains at the moment, but I think that was to be expected because there is less consumer demand, for several reasons. The sport has spread tremendously, for one thing, and also people are now worried about the ecology and about the environment in general, which means that the industry is going to have difficulties, not too serious ones I hope, and will have to adapt to the change in consumer attitudes.
However I should like to remind the hon. member for Charlevoix that there is a considerable export surplus of Canadian snowmobiles, amounting to over $50 million in 1972.
It is true that, as some hon. members have said recently, snowmobile imports have risen, but exports have also risen. The main reason for the rise in imports is consumer preferences.

Mr. Speaker, as I said a while ago, it is nice to speak on this motion and to see that all parties in the House agree that it was a good agreement that Canada entered into in 1965. It is also nice to see that once again the Liberal party at that time fulfilled its role as the party of the sixties.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
It is nice to remind hon. members that the Liberal Party brought this agreement about and is still very proud of it. I am glad that members on all sides of the House agree with the agreement.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party was the party of the sixties for the automobile industry and from the point of view of industrial policy for Canada and good social policies. All that we discuss in this House lately is reaction to what the Liberals have done in the past and what they are doing now. Once again, we have political parties not coming out with new programs but just responding or reacting to what the Liberals do. This is very significant in Canadian politics-in the sixties as in the seventies- because when we speak about social policy, industrial policy, all the other political parties have to do is react or respond to what we propose. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: We talked about that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT

Canada-United, States Auto Pact

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: So what are you going to do about it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: In 1964, when the hon. member's friends were in power, the price differential at the factory level was 17 per cent. That is what it was just before 1964. The Liberal party came to power in 1963 and within a few months it said, "We must do something about this problem." We did something, Mr. Speaker, because now the price gap has shrunk from 17 per cent to 8.5 per cent.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: That is why you pay more than $200 more for a car in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Well, you people should make up your minds; either you agree with these devices or you do not. Even though they have asked in their testimony given before the United States prices commission for a 3 per cent increase, the automobile manufacturers gave a public commitment in this country not to increase the price of 1973 models in Canada. They gave this commitment even though they wanted to increase the price of 1973 models by 3 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The companies have lied before and they may continue to lie.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
One can assume that if they had wanted to increase the price by only 3 per cent the price differential would have shrunk. If they can increase the price on one side of the border by 3 per cent, it means that the price differential here has shrunk by 3 per cent.
The other commitment the automobile manufacturers gave to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was that in subsequent years they would take into consideration the intention of this government to reduce the price differential. In other words, they have given a commitment that they will work toward shrinking the price differential between United States and Canadian cars. So, Mr. Speaker, that famous price gap has been reduced from 17 per cent to 8.5 per cent and because of the actions of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce the price spread will be reduced further. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce obtained those commitments immediately after his appointment. I think it is important to remember that.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Don't blush.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: I notice that the members of the Conservative party did not have much to say in this debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) said that the government employs skilled negotiators but that the Tories should be in power. Let us remember that when they were in power before 1964 the gap was 17 per cent. All the Conservatives did in this debate was compliment the Liberal Party for the good auto pact and for having such skilled negotiators. I was
(Mr. Orlikow.]
happy to hear Conservative members say that. Some said that the pact is of vital importance to our secondary manufacturing industries. We agree, and we are happy that they agree with us.
I now come to the proposal made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. I find it interesting. If I understood him correctly, he is all for abandoning the safeguard provisions of 1964. As I understand it, he proposed other safeguards. Jean-Luc Pepin said for two or three years, as others have said, that they are not important and they were not a significant factor in the negotiations. It is clear that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby retracted the comments he made in the last two or three years. He suggested that the safeguards are not good any more and that we need new safeguards.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I think I am on solid ground in saying that the hon. member is attributing words to me that I did not utter. The point I made was not that we should abandon the 1964 safeguards; it was, and I hope the hon. member was listening, that instead of abandoning them we should raise the level of safeguards from the 1964 level to one applicable in 1973. Even for a Liberal member that should be reasonably easy to grasp.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The hon. member should have made that clear in his speech, because that is not what I understood him to say. I contend that the hon. member is no longer saying what he has said for two years. He has changed. We are happy to see it because we hope that all parties will follow the Liberal party in its thinking. We are happy to see this development. The hon. member said that we should abandon the tariff protection affecting consumers-I am trying to remember what I heard the hon. member say. He said we should include those cars that are bought by Canadians in the United States as consumption from the point of view of calculating the production and consumption safeguards. The hon. member went on to another safeguard which would raise the value of the Canadian content from the 1964 level to the 1972 level. I listened to the hon. member.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: The hon. member said that he was not in favour of abandoning any safeguards. He certainly abandoned his insistence that the 1964 safeguards be kept. He now wants to have another level of production for 1972. I just want to make sure that the hon. member is adopting a more realistic and practical policy on this question. What happens if we reduce or abandon the tariffs and do not get to the safeguards? Is this a packet? The hon. member said it was a packet.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the parliamentary secretary, but the time allotted to him has expired.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my remarks this evening will be rather brief as my time is very limited. I wish to correct a few remarks made by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn). My understand-
March 13, 1973

ing is that the cost of automobiles throughout Canada is the same and that delivery charges in Canada from the plant to the various outlets are prorated across the total production costs. There may be some differences with respect to the price that individual dealers pay for cars, but that is largely a question of volume. The difference really amounts to a question of competition and volume in the area; it has nothing to do with the price at the plant.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Is the hon. member rising on a point of order?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. This is very important. I made a statement to the effect that car buyers in British Columbia and car buyers in Nova Scotia, generally speaking, have to pay more for automobiles. The hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) just said that this in fact is not true. I wish to have some facts and figures to back up his argument.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: Order, please. That is more a question of debate than a question of privilege.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
One of the other matters that affects the price in Canada is the fact that distribution, in terms of advertising material, is required in both English and French. From the point of view of this party, that is a proper charge against the price of distribution of cars and should continue. It has something to do with the difference in cost.
These two matters, prorating the delivery cost throughout Canada and the cost of sales material in English and French, cannot in any way explain an 8.5 per cent difference in the cost of automobiles to Canadian consumers. We might talk about a point or a point and a half, but certainly not 8.5 per cent. There is no question, from the information given to us by dealers in Buffalo and other points in the United States who receive cars manufactured in Canada, that cars manufactured here are put together better and are wanted by their customers in greater number than cars manufactured in the United States. Our information is that cars produced in Canada are, in fact, better automobiles.
The minister should have interfered in this matter long ago. He should have got together with automobile companies, which are really a massive oligopoly, and clearly stated that Canadians are not going to be ripped-off any longer by this government or by them.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext: It is a corporate rip-off.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAYS S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP AN IMPROVED CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTOMOTIVE AGREEMENT
speechtext:
In the long run, in terms of trade, the auto pact with the United States has been of great advantage to Canada. This afternoon and this evening the matter of trade in snowmobiles was mentioned. There is no question that that trade has produced advantages to Canada. However, when we deal with these automobile companies it disturbs me greatly to see the prices of the parts used to put a car together.
Adjournment Debate
The last time I looked at the cost of putting an ordinary automobile together by buying parts from distributors of the three large automobile manufacturers, I found that it would cost between $50,000 and $60,000 to manufacture a car. If the minister and this government had any concern about the cost to the Canadian consumer, they would direct their attention to the rip-off that Canadians are receiving in terms of the activity of the three or perhaps four large automobile manufacturers.
When talking to the leader of one of the automobile companies he mentioned the cost that Canadian production must face with respect to imports from foreign countries. He pointed out that when companies in Japan deliver cars to Canada, the excise of tariff charges are determined on the manufacturing costs, whereas the sales cost or sales tax paid by the manufacturer in Canada not only includes the manufacturing cost but also the cost of the distribution system, auvertising and transportation.
It is clear that this government should listen to the representations of the companies and organize excise charges so that Canadian manufacturers are not discriminated against compared with foreign manufacturers. When the minister is dealing with the automobile companies and forcing them to control their prices, I suggest that he look closely at the excise tax arrangements in connection with charges made on the importation of automobiles.
I note the time is ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 15 I put a question to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) in connection with the Law of the Sea Conference to be held in Chile, I believe, in 1974. The question arose out of my conviction-I think it is one which is shared by most Canadians, certainly by those living in the eastern provinces-that this conference is likely to be the most important ever held from the point of view of the Atlantic region and, in particular, the province of N ewf oundland.
The issue of conservation, which will certainly be one of the subjects under discussion, affects directly or indirectly the lives of almost all Canadians living on our east coast. The fishing industry affects, directly and indirectly, virtually every living soul in Newfoundland and Labrador. The fishing industry is the largest single employer in Newfoundland. Of a total work force numbering slightly over 150,000, 20,000 people are engaged in the fishing

industry. With this in mind, Mr. Speaker, you will appreciate my concern as to the position to be taken by the government at the forthcoming conference.
I believe we must take a strong and definite position, because unless we can induce other fishing nations to agree to some form of management control and conservation the fishing industry off our east coast will be seriously endangered. If this were to happen, the livelihood of a large segment of our population would be affected and the economy of the region would suffer a serious decline.
As a Newfoundlander, I am especially concerned about this conference for another reason. As we all know, the continental shelf equals about 40 per cent of the land mass of Canada. This is a valuable piece of real estate. For Newfoundland it is particularly important since a large chunk of that continental shelf is on the doorstep, as it were, of my province. I refer to the Grand Banks. In Newfoundland-and I presume a similar situation exists in other eastern provinces-we have seen a very serious decline in total fish landings. The situation has grown progressively worse since 1968. In 1972, the catch showed a sharp decline amounting to approximately 26 per cent compared with 1971. In 1971, landings in Newfoundland were down by 12 per cent compared with 1970. In 1968, the total was 950 million pounds of fish compared with 650 million pounds in 1972. It is therefore not hard to understand why we are so uptight with respect to the forthcoming Law of the Sea Conference.
We want to be sure that Canada's case is well prepared, that our Minister of Fisheries and his officials develop a dialogue with people of the fishing industry. We want to be sure that he will draw upon the most qualified people in Canada in respect of fisheries, and that the expertise of fish merchants in eastern and western Canada is available in order to make sure we present the most solid case imaginable in dealing with foreign nations in an effort to bring about a sane approach to the fishing industry. In that way we could head off what we think, and what scientists tell us, will eventually be the depletion of our sea resources unless the wholesale raiding now taking place by foreign countries off our Grand Banks and continental shelf is stopped.
I realize that the minister has only three minutes in which to reply, but I hope he will give us some idea of what our position will be at the conference. I hope he will tell us whether an agenda has been agreed upon and whether Canada's representatives to the conference have been appointed. I hope he will indicate whether he has sought the advice of the fishing industry-

subtopic: FISHERIES-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON POSITION TO BE TAKEN BY CANADA AT LAW OF THE SEA CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the next Law of the Sea Conference is going to be very important for Canada. The main reason is that we have the second longest coastline in the world and the world's largest continental shelf. Much of the world's shipping passes close to our shores. We have a very important fishing industry on both coasts which can also be affected by pollution. Canada's attitude at the next Law of the Sea Conference, therefore, must be that of a nation which is

concerned about the protection of its long shoreline and its large and productive continental shelf area.
This concern can be listed under two headings. The first is protection from pollution, and the other is the wise management and conservation of its fishing resource. Canada co-sponsored the resolution in the United Nations last fall setting up the next Law of the Sea Conference, its organization meeting in New York in November, 1973, and its first substantial meeting dealing with policy to be held in Santiago, Chile, beginning in April, 1974. Canada's position is, and must be, that of a coastal state. This is being re-enforced in two preparatory meetings to be held during the course of this spring and summer, one dealing with marine pollution and the other with fisheries.
In respect of marine pollution, we will be pursuing the principles which Canada sponsored and which were successfully adopted at the United Nations' Conference on the Human Environment, in Stockholm. Essentially, Canada's position was that the interest of a coastal state must not only be protected, but the coastal nation must have certain powers to reach out and, if necessary, to apprehend vessels in trouble, like oil tankers, etc. This is a new power and one that would not have been tolerated by maritime nations a decade or so ago. In any event, that principle is gaining recognition. We hope it will become well established in international law as a result of the next Law of the Sea Conference.
In respect of fisheries, our basic approach is that coastal states should have jurisdiction out to the edge of their continental shelf, and indeed down the slope of those shelves, over all living resources of the sea as well as the mineral resources. That has been our approach and it is the approach we put forward at the FAO conference recently in Vancouver which was attended by all of the fishing nations of the world.

ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-KILLING OF POLICEMEN-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION TO RESTRICT FURTHER SALE AND DISTRIBUTION OF FIREARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 17 this year I directed a question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) which I felt was vital and important, particularly in view of the public concern about safety. This question dealt with the possibility of the regulation of firearms in this country. The question is as follows:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Justice. It is also prompted by the incident-
I was referring to the incident in Toronto of the most recent death of a police officer.
-in Toronto. In view of the increasing homicides occurring as a result of the use of rifles in this country, is the minister considering legislation to restrict further the sale and distribution of firearms?
The minister's answer at that time was:
Mr. Speaker, that question is one which is under constant consid-
March 13, 1973

eration and review. The House had an opportunity to address itself to it not long ago, and the government will be addressing itself further to that question.
I was very pleased, after that question was asked, that on February 22 the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) asked a similar question of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) whose answer at that time was that this is being considered; in other words, the further control of weapons is being considered. I say this is an important issue because of the volume of mail which I believe all members have been receiving about the concern of the public for the increasing crime rate and the murder rate, which has increased 53 per cent over a period of ten years.
I would particularly refer the minister to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics study for the period 1960 to 1969 which deals with the use of firearms and the number of murders which took place in that period. It is interesting to note that in that period 1,174 people were murdered, with firearms being the weapon. That represented 44 per cent of all murders in that period. Of those murders in which firearms were involved, some 72 per cent involved the use of rifles. The main point I want to bring home to the minister is, as the minister well knows, that the rifle is a completely unrestricted weapon at this time.
I remember having had occasion to defend a young man in British Columbia who attempted to murder his fiancee. He missed her by a very small margin. After investigation it was found that this man had attempted suicide on several occasions. In his home he had at least four rifles, and so far as I know, after having served his sentence he still has complete access to weapons. I believe this represents a serious defect in our laws.
When a person, for example, who has been committed voluntarily to a mental hospital and is released, there is nothing to restrict him from purchasing a weapon should any of his paranoic delusions overcome him and his mental disorder get the better of him from time to time. This happens. There is no law at present which restricts any man from purchasing a rifle. I shall not bore the minister too much longer with statistics.
Needless to say, there is overwhelming evidence that the United Kingdom, which has good, firm weapon control legislation, has a lower murder rate generally in connection with firearms. It is interesting, for example, to compare the cities in the United States. New york, which has a fairly respectable Sullivan law, has a 25 per cent murder rate by firearms, whereas Dallas, where unrestricted use of firearms is allowed, has a rate of 72 per cent of murders by firearms.
Those who oppose the further restriction of weapons usually use the argument that it is people who are responsible for the murders, not guns. This is a fallacious argument because what gun control legislation, in effect, does is to license people. It is almost a euphemism to say that one is licensing guns. The permit to carry a weapon goes to the person. I would think that in any sane, sensible and civilized society a person with a serious history of mental illness, a previous criminal record or a history of domestic instability should be denied access to weapons.
In the city that I represent, the coroner over the past three years investigated 24 homicides, 20 of which were caused by firearms. Some of them were accidental. Never-

theless, the problem is not insignificant-it is overwhelming. It is estimated that we have six million weapons in this country and about 600,000 registered handguns. Quite frankly, I am tired of the gun lobby.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-KILLING OF POLICEMEN-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION TO RESTRICT FURTHER SALE AND DISTRIBUTION OF FIREARMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the fact that the hon. member is raising this question again so that I can make our position quite clear in the House-which I certainly made quite clear outside the House and which did not appear in Hansard-that I would not support changes in the law which simply add a tremendous amount of red tape without doing anything to keep guns from people who are dangerous. The hon. member made an interesting case which, if read carefully, shows that murder by knife is a nicer game than murder by gun. I cannot quite see the point of that. The point I am making is that people who are unbalanced may well find another weapon than a gun, and the hon. member has to prove why it is important to go through the whole restriction process and what good it will do us.
There are honourable and honest uses of weapons for hunting, for target practice and in sport. If you want to begin to license everybody and to impose a licensing system, you have to ask what good you are going to do. Are you going to have a situation where people will inevitably, quite innocently, be in possession of guns contrary to the rules? The hon. member proposed Bill C-138, so he turned his mind to the question. In it I see, among other things, that he would make it an offence to even lend a gun to another person without a permit, so that if two of my friends are in the same duck blind together and want to exchange shotguns for one or two moments, they are contravening his rules. Obviously you have to examine and change that. Surely he would admit that thousands of people would be in contravention of this kind of law quite innocently and be good citizens at the same time.
The point I am making is that we are quite prepared to examine this law in order to see whether we could stiffen the penalty in relation to the misuse of weapons. That is the important point. Until it is proven to me that the rules and regulations will in fact do the job, I will not see them in place to hamper and harass innocent citizens. It is of course quite typical of the party which the hon. member represents-I see it in the province of British Columbia and in the province of Saskatchewan-to introduce laws which ban everything and then by permit or special dispensation to someone whom they like we get back a little bit of what has been banned. This kind of rule by decree, by some kind of divine ordinance of some expert, imposed upon the people by an NDP government is seen in B.C. in regard to land, in regard to every new venture. I am not surprised to see it in the hon. member's bill.
I say to him that if he can show me at any time a rule or a change which, without creating a lot of red tape, a lot of harassment, will produce a good result, I will support him on it. We will introduce changes which will improve the protection of our citizens, but not changes which will

MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-REQUEST THAT MEMBERS BE BETTER INFORMED CONCERNING PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 13, 1973, I asked a question concerning the Local Initiatives Program, as can be read on page 771 of Hansard. I then asked that hon. members be better acquainted with the procedure relating to local initiative projects.
Mr. Speaker, in this regard, I will quote some precise facts. On February 16, I wrote to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), responsible before the House for the LIP program, in order to ask him what stage some forty projects had reached. I did not get any answer.
On February 19, I put on the order paper questions Nos. 1010, 1011 and 1016 concerning the development of extremely important projects in my area. I did not get any answer either. However, there seems to be no more money available. According to the minister's statement, the approval period is over and he can give overall statistics to the House.
Moreover, while one hon. member does not know what happened to some projects within his own riding, the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), who has nothing to do with it, is so much aware of what is going on that he can readily write to people and tell them, which is very serious, that the project has been accepted and that it will obtain the funds required for implementation. A few days later the project sponsors receive another letter from the co-ordinator of the Local Initiative Program to the effect that the projects are rejected.
I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacGuigan) to the fact that it is illogical to give wrong information on the development of a project to hon. members. Whoever we are we have to come up with answers for the project directors. We support the principle of local initiatives and I want this to be clear: We agree to this kind of program. Consequently, it would be normal for the department involved to inform us as to the progress of each project about which citizens inquire. Also we would like to know why certain projects have been rejected and others accepted because, after all, they involve the expenditure of tax money.
We would like to know whether it would be possible to review the local initiative projects. No satisfactory reply can be obtained from the department on this subject. Some say yes, some say no and finally we do not know where we stand. The Minister of Transport could probably obtain this information but hon. members are unable to get it.
I want to protest strongly against this situation. We are not here to play politics, to announce that projects have been accepted or for political gain; we leave this to the government and in particular to the Minister of Transport who is quite successful at it.
We have been elected to serve as a link between our constituents and the department and the government, and, along that line, I intend to act equitably and honestly to the end. This is the reason why I should like to dwell on that point tonight. I can anticipate already the reply of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. He will tell me that a special service, a departmental section has been established in order to supply answers to hon. members, that such a service is very good, that the officials are writing hon. members to find out what they think. Mr. Speaker, I swear that we will let him know what we think, for we intend to get replies, not of a political character but of an administrative character, that is to say honest replies, allowing us as members to efficiently serve our people. In that respect, I again offer my co-operation to that department. On the other hand, I expect as much from it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MANPOWER-LOCAL INITIATIVES PROGRAM-REQUEST THAT MEMBERS BE BETTER INFORMED CONCERNING PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be some confusion about the procedure which is followed in letting hon. members know about LIP applications. I regret that I perhaps contributed to this confusion by an answer I gave to the House in the minister's absence on January 30 in which I suggested that members were not being informed. What I had in mind was that they are not informed before the announcement is made, and I think perhaps this confused the issue.
Let me therefore review the procedure, which is as follows. All members of parliament were consulted at an early stage of consideration of LIP projects and then, after the official decision had been made by the department, the members were advised by the special information group of the department of projects approved for their constituencies.
Whenever a project was approved in the constituency of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), he received a letter from the special information group informing him of it. If an hon. member wished to know the status of a LIP application before a decision was made, he had the right to call the special information group. I think the telephone number and address of this group was made available to all members.
When a project was approved, I do not think there was any problem. The difficulty seemed to arise in those cases where the application was not approved as members were not notified of this fact. The extra personnel required to carry out this service would have doubled the staff of the special information group, but personally I believe that members should be so notified in any future program of this kind, even at extra cost. The onus to find out the reasons why projects were not approved was put on members. Within the limitations imposed by the budget for this year, the fact is that every attempt was made to keep members informed on an objective basis of programs which were approved, and in those cases where they were not, members had the right to inquire and be given the fullest information.
